It tells you, for every RMiT requirement, what AWS is responsible for and what you implement. The compliance guides published by AWS SAS over the past year provide implementation guidance for International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standards that complements the workbook. These guides show how to implement controls that meet the requirements of specific standards and frameworks using AWS services, giving your technical and compliance teams a clear path from regulatory expectation to deployed architecture. Malaysian financial institutions can now trace from BNM regulatory requirement, through AWS control implementation, to the evidence that demonstrates it: AWS third-party attestations for AWS-side controls, and your own workload evidence for customer-side controls. AWS maintains redundant network connectivity with multiple tier-1 transit providers across each Availability Zone. 10.49: (Customer responsibility) Customer Well-Architected REL 2: How do you plan your network topology? Implement multi-AZ deployments. Configure VPC flow logs and use AWS Network Firewall. For your workload, use evidence from your own environment, including configurations, logs, and AWS Config conformance pack results. Auditors can also use the guides as a reference for how a control is typically implemented on AWS. AWS SAS has published five compliance guides over the past year. Each guide provides control-level implementation guidance on the customer side of the Shared Responsibility Model, showing how AWS services can be configured to meet the requirements of specific standards and frameworks. Download the relevant ISO compliance guides to plan how you implement your customer-side controls. Download AWS ISO certificates and SOC reports from AWS Artifact for AWS-side evidence. items.summary_html:
Your next Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) notification submission needs auditable evidence of how Amazon Web Services (AWS) controls align with Risk Management in Technology (RMiT) requirements. Two resources now exist to support that work: the AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT and the compliance guides published by AWS Security Assurance Services (AWS SAS).

The AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT, available through AWS Artifact, maps each RMiT provision to AWS Control Objectives (AWS responsibilities under the AWS Shared Responsibility Model) and AWS Well-Architected Framework best practices (your responsibilities). It tells you, for every RMiT requirement, what AWS is responsible for and what you implement.

The compliance guides published by AWS SAS over the past year provide implementation guidance for International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standards that complements the workbook. These guides show how to implement controls that meet the requirements of specific standards and frameworks using AWS services, giving your technical and compliance teams a clear path from regulatory expectation to deployed architecture.

Malaysian financial institutions can now trace from BNM regulatory requirement, through AWS control implementation, to the evidence that demonstrates it: AWS third-party attestations for AWS-side controls, and your own workload evidence for customer-side controls. BNM expects this specificity in notification documentation.

AWS Workbook for BNM RMiT

The workbook is a structured Excel document available through AWS Artifact. For each of the 394 RMiT provisions, it identifies:

  • Whether the requirement is an AWS responsibility or a customer responsibility under the Shared Responsibility Model
  • The specific AWS Control Objective that addresses the requirement (where AWS is responsible)
  • The relevant AWS Well-Architected Framework best practice for customer implementation (where the customer is responsible)
  • Supporting information and references for each mapping

The following is a sample entry from the workbook:

RMiT Requirement Responsibility Source AWS supporting information 10.49: A financial institution should ensure network resilience… AWS AWS Control Objectives AWS Control Section: Network Security. AWS maintains redundant network connectivity with multiple tier-1 transit providers across each Availability Zone. 10.49: (Customer responsibility) Customer Well-Architected REL 2: How do you plan your network topology? Implement multi-AZ deployments. Configure VPC flow logs and use AWS Network Firewall.

The workbook currently includes 394 rows across all RMiT appendix requirements, with 208 mapped to AWS responsibilities and 186 to customer responsibilities.

Why this matters now

BNM revised RMiT guidelines effective 28 November 2025, and updated them on 25 September 2026 to add requirements for National Critical Information Infrastructure (NCII) entities. Financial institutions operating under both BNM Outsourcing and BNM RMiT must demonstrate that their cloud service providers maintain controls aligned with regulatory expectations. Institutions preparing notification submissions for material cloud workloads need auditable evidence of this alignment.

The revised guidelines set higher expectations for evidence quality. Institutions submitting notifications without clear, structured control mapping evidence might face extended review cycles and requests for additional information from BNM. Workloads that could be deployed in weeks remain in governance queues for months when supporting documentation lacks the specificity regulators expect.

Compliance guides from AWS Security Assurance Services

Start with the RMiT workbook to identify which provisions AWS addresses and which you implement. Then use the following compliance guides to design and implement your customer-side controls. The guides are implementation guidance for your teams. Audit evidence comes from two places. For AWS-side controls, use AWS third-party attestations, such as ISO certificates and System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports, available in AWS Artifact. For your workload, use evidence from your own environment, including configurations, logs, and AWS Config conformance pack results. Auditors can also use the guides as a reference for how a control is typically implemented on AWS.

AWS SAS has published five compliance guides over the past year. Each guide provides control-level implementation guidance on the customer side of the Shared Responsibility Model, showing how AWS services can be configured to meet the requirements of specific standards and frameworks. These guides were written by AWS SAS practicing security assessors and auditors holding Payment Card Industry Qualified Security Assessor (PCI QSA), Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP), Certified Information Security Manager (CISM), ISO 27001 Lead Auditor, and Certified Cloud Security Professional (CCSP) certifications, drawing on experience from hundreds of cloud security assessments across financial services globally.

The following is the list of guides AWS SAS practicing auditors have published, which include control mapping information relevant to BNM RMiT:

  • ISO/IEC 27001:2022 on AWS (Information Security Management) – Maps Annex A controls to AWS services
  • ISO 31000:2018 on AWS (Risk Management) – Integrates AWS services into risk identification, assessment, treatment, and monitoring
  • ISO/IEC 42001:2023 on AWS (Artificial Intelligence Management Systems) – Supports institutions building responsible artificial intelligence (AI) on AWS
  • Cloud Security Alliance Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM) v4.1 on AWS (Cloud Security Controls) – Maps 207 control objectives to AWS
  • American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) SOC 2 on AWS – Navigates SOC 2 compliance using AWS services
How these resources work together

A Malaysian financial institution preparing a BNM notification can use these resources together:

  • The RMiT workbook identifies which RMiT provisions are AWS responsibilities and which are customer responsibilities.
  • For AWS responsibilities, the workbook references the specific AWS Control Objective.
  • AWS third-party reports in AWS Artifact, such as the AWS ISO/IEC 27001 certificate and SOC reports, attest to those AWS Control Objectives. For customer responsibilities, the ISO compliance guides show how to implement the corresponding controls using AWS services.
  • The ISO 31000 guide can inform the risk management methodology you apply to your cloud workloads.
  • AWS Config Conformance Packs for BNM RMiT provide automated, continuous monitoring of deployed controls.

Resources also supporting this approach:

  • The AWS User Guide for Financial Institutions in Malaysia examines the BNM Outsourcing and RMiT policy documents and sets out the steps to launch regulated workloads on AWS
  • AWS Config Conformance Packs for BNM RMiT provide automated compliance monitoring through managed AWS Config rules mapped to specific RMiT controls

Compliance teams across Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) financial services have already begun referencing the AWS Guide to BNM RMiT and associated resources in their cloud risk assessment processes and BNM notification documentation.

Looking ahead: AI governance

For institutions deploying generative AI and machine learning, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (Artificial Intelligence Management Systems) is relevant to BNM technology governance expectations. In November 2024, AWS became the first major cloud provider to announce ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI services. AWS passed its first surveillance audit in November 2025 with zero findings. The ISO 42001 compliance guide published in May 2026 supports institutions building their own responsible AI systems on their side of the AWS Shared Responsibility Model.

How to get started
  • Access the RMiT workbook through AWS Artifact and review with your compliance lead to identify which provisions apply to your material cloud workloads.
  • Download the relevant ISO compliance guides to plan how you implement your customer-side controls. Download AWS ISO certificates and SOC reports from AWS Artifact for AWS-side evidence.
  • Map your workload-specific controls using the workbook as the RMiT baseline and the ISO guides as implementation guidance.
  • Implement automated compliance monitoring using the BNM RMiT conformance pack for AWS Config to maintain continuous visibility over your control posture.
  • Engage your AWS account team or AWS SAS for additional guidance on implementing customer-side controls referenced in the workbook.

As BNM updates its regulatory expectations, AWS will update these resources to reflect revised requirements. Subscribe to the AWS Security Blog for update notifications.

Additional resources
  • AWS Financial Services Compliance Center for Malaysia
  • AWS Artifact (access the RMiT Workbook and ISO certifications)
  • ISO/IEC 27001:2022 on AWS Compliance Guide
  • ISO 31000:2018 Risk Management on AWS Compliance Guide
  • ISO/IEC 42001:2023 on AWS Compliance Guide (AI Management Systems)
  • Cloud Security Alliance CCM v4.1 on AWS Compliance Guide
  • AICPA SOC 2 Compliance Guide on AWS
  • AWS Guide to BNM RMiT
  • AWS User Guide for Financial Institutions in Malaysia
  • AWS Shared Responsibility Model
  • AWS Well-Architected Framework
  • Operational Best Practices for BNM RMiT (AWS Config)

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

He has 20 years of experience in technology risk, audit, and information security, including leading a cloud risk team in financial services. items.summary_html:
Welcome to volume fifty-one of Scrolls, a newsletter for sharing cool stuff from the IndieWeb & Cybersecurity realms. This week we’re getting to know some of our fellow humans on the web, and we do some of the usual shaking-of-our-heads in cyberland.

Cozy up, it’s time to scroll!

IndieWeb

The year is 2026 (almost 2027!), it’s time for you to make a website — a little digital home for you, and all your stuff, on the Internet. It’ll be a place you love to be, and perhaps others too! It really is the in thing to do right now y’know? You will never be alone on the human side of the web.

So go connect with your fellow humans on the web. Read their blogs. Get to know them. They’re tons of us out there. The web is in fact not entirely terrible slop, commercialization and sadness.

Small Web Finds and Features

Let’s see what I found in the abyss on the web recently!

  • Adel Faure’s site is what you can never have on big social, or big tech or big whatever. It’s glorious. An awesome example of creativity and what you can do with a personal website. Go there now and get lost a bit. I would recommend roaming the pixel art halls first 😃
  • A blog/personal site is a great place for lists. Any kind of lists. Here’s one for musicals
  • I know I’m not the only person who read Animorphs growing up, but it’s fun to see it mentioned
  • Starbase430 — a stellar outpost for the Indieweb 🪐
  • So you have a website yeah? That’s cool. But do you have a wobsite?
  • Is anyone there? (on the web). In my experience — yes!
  • (Near) Infinite TV courtesy of the Internet Archive
Cybersecurity

A couple interesting bits from the cyberworld this week…

  • eMudhra’s full incident report is as sad as we all expected it to be
  • Mozilla released their fingerprinting study which is a pretty fascinating read
  • Learn about DKIM2
  • Security vendors are rightly scolded for breaking embargoes with their li’l marketing blog posts

Thanks for reading Scrolls! Good night!

TheMailer – Self-hosted Phishing Platform that runs on Claude and ChatGPT
items.summary: TheMailer, a self-hosted phishing platform identified by Varonis Threat Labs, brings commercial AI models into almost every stage of an email attack. Rather than only fixing grammar or writing convincing messages, it uses AI to build lures, change templates, test delivery, and manage replies. Operators supply their own API keys to connect services including Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, Mistral, and DeepSeek. According to the research, TheMailer has been advertised on a cybercrime network since March 2026. Its sales thread has attracted more than 24,000 views, although that figure does not confirm customer numbers or successful attacks. Advertised lifetime licenses range from $3,000 to $6,000, depending on the package and whether it includes AI modules. TheMailer Forum Sales Advertisement (Image Source: Varonis) Buyers receive installation help and support, while supplying their own mail servers, proxies, and target lists. A Telegram sales channel and automated cryptocurrency payment bot help handle purchases. The setup reduces the technical work needed to start a campaign by packaging email delivery and AI tools in an interface that resembles ordinary marketing software. The approach builds on tools such as SpamGPT, an AI-powered phishing platform , which combines message generation, mail account management, delivery testing, and campaign tracking. TheMailer takes that model further by linking AI rewriting directly to feedback about where test messages land. That connection turns content creation into an ongoing process rather than a single preparation step. Its most notable feature, Inbox Loop, sends a test email and checks a connected mailbox through IMAP to determine whether the message reached the inbox or spam folder. When a test lands in spam, the platform asks AI to rewrite the template and tries again. This tests delivery conditions, but does not guarantee access to every recipient’s inbox. TheMailer Campaign Management Dashboard (Image Source: Varonis) The Varonis Threat Labs report describes an AI Letter Builder that creates HTML email from short prompts. It can also import genuine messages from a connected mailbox and use them as templates. This gives attackers an easy starting point for copying familiar brand layouts and language without designing each lure themselves. Templates and subject lines can be rewritten for individual recipients. One example uses a Robinhood account warning with a changing reference number. Other presets turn messages into security alerts or routine transaction notices. Options advertised as removing “AI patterns” aim to make the wording seem human, but the report does not establish that these options reliably defeat detection. An AI Autopilot module groups recipients by mailbox provider and applies provider-specific sending limits and content guidance. Supported groups include Gmail, Microsoft, GMX, Yandex, and French providers. A screenshot shows a list containing 145,133 entries, largely Japanese business and university domains. That is evidence of a displayed target list, not proof that those organizations were compromised. List containing 145,133 entries (Image Source: Varonis) The platform also advertises account warm-up, delivery testing, and reply management. AI WarmUP appears designed to exchange messages between sending accounts so they look established. Inbox Finder tests delivery settings against a seed mailbox. A separate reply manager gathers responses and offers AI sorting and answering, extending automation beyond the initial message. TheMailer’s attachment tools convert HTML templates into personalized PDFs, including filenames based on recipient names. Embedded links and changing metadata produce files with different hashes, making simple file blocklists less useful. Other features create SVG redirects and calendar invitations. Branding shown in sample lures includes Robinhood and IONOS, alongside financial alerts and hotel booking callback themes. The delivery features include randomized headers, sender profiles, and redirects that place trusted Google domains ahead of another destination. These features can complicate review, but a familiar opening domain does not make the final page safe. Likewise, changing a message or file hash does not remove the phishing request or stop deeper analysis of its links and behavior. The main defensive lesson is to assess intent, identity, and behavior rather than writing style alone. As explained in Cybersecurity News’ coverage of AI-written phishing detection , identifying machine-written text is different from identifying a malicious request. Teams should check sender history, authentication results, reply-address mismatches, redirect chains, and attachment behavior. Unexpected requests for passwords, payments, or verification codes deserve review even when every sentence looks natural. Staff should verify sensitive requests through a known contact channel rather than details supplied in the message. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Agenda!

items.title: Run Your Qualys Program by Conversation, Inside Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise
items.summary: Qualys ROCky for Gemini Enterprise, now available on Google Cloud Marketplace, allows you to ask your vulnerability, asset, and risk questions, get an answer ranked by real risk, and act on it, without leaving Gemini Enterprise. With the introduction of frontier AI models, vulnerabilities are now being discovered and weaponized at machine speed. Unfortunately, most security teams still triage at human speed. A typical enterprise carries thousands of open findings and can fix only a small fraction of them, yet leadership still expects a straight answer to a simple question: Are we keeping up? Getting that answer usually means exporting a scan, building a spreadsheet, and losing an afternoon. Today, we are live with Qualys ROCky for Gemini Enterprise . It puts your Qualys vulnerability, asset, and risk data one question away, right inside Gemini Enterprise, and it can even take the next step in the process for you, with a person in control of any changes to an asset. Your Program, By Conversation The agent turns interactions with the Qualys Enterprise TruRisk Platform into a conversation. Four things it does well: Ask about your data. “Which of my internet-facing hosts is the biggest risk?” “Are we exposed to Log4Shell?” “What is tied to ransomware?” Whatever your risk management question, you get an answer from your subscription in seconds, in plain language, rather than a raw export. Prioritize by real risk. Ask what to fix first, and the agent returns a worklist ranked by the Qualys Enterprise TruRisk score. It surfaces the handful of vulnerabilities that are actively exploited, listed in the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, or associated with ransomware, and it explains why each one matters. Half a day of specialist triage becomes a two-minute, defensible decision. Remediate with confirmation. When you are ready to act, the agent stages a patch job in TruRisk Eliminate and shows exactly what will deploy, patch stability, and to how many assets. Nothing changes a host until you explicitly say yes. You go from finding to fixing in the same conversation, with a clear record of who approved what. Prove you are keeping up. Ask for your mean time to remediate, how your open CISA KEV backlog is aging, or how current your scan data is, and the agent answers on demand, in the terms boards and auditors expect. items.title: Critical Java 17 RCE Vulnerability Puts Servers at Risk as Oracle Releases 11 Security Fixes
items.summary: A remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in Java 17 has prompted warnings for server admins, especially as Oracle released 11 new Java SE security updates on the same day. The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-114938. Public reports say it needs no login and affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later. The details are still unconfirmed. Security firm watchTowr said on X that it is aware of public reports of an unauthenticated RCE in Java. It told teams to review their Java environments and watch for vendor news. Reports rate the flaw 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0, which is Critical. South Korea’s National Intelligence Service sent a warning to public bodies about a Java flaw that could allow remote code execution without authentication. Open questions remain. The CVE record is still reserved with no public description. Early reports point to memory corruption. No fixed build, proof-of-concept code or sign of real-world exploitation has been published. The reports also don’t name the weak component or say whether a special setup is needed. Running Java 17 does not prove you are exposed. Risk depends on whether outside data can reach the weak code. What Oracle Fixed in November Oracle’s November 2026 Critical Security Patch Update covers 652 new patches across its products. Java SE gets 11 of them, and all can be used over a network without credentials. The highest CVSS 3.1 score among them is 8.1. Fixes also cover GraalVM and JavaFX. Oracle lists these builds as affected: Java SE 8u511, 11.0.33, 17.0.21, 21.0.13, 25.0.5 and 27.0.1. It has not tied any of the 11 fixes to CVE-2026-114938. Oracle’s JDK release notes are the place to find the replacement builds. Astra also notes that a secondary report lists 17.0.21.1 and 21.0.13.1 as scheduled releases. Product / Line Affected version (per source) Patched version OpenJDK 17 (CVE-2026-114938) 17.0.6 and later Java 17 updates Not published Oracle Java SE 8 8u511, 8u511-perf Not published Oracle Java SE 11 11.0.33 Not published Oracle Java SE 17 17.0.21 Not published (17.0.21.1 reportedly scheduled) Oracle Java SE 21 21.0.13 Not published (21.0.13.1 reportedly scheduled) Oracle Java SE 25 25.0.5 Not published Oracle Java SE 27 27.0.1 Not published Oracle GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21, 21.0.13 Not published Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20.0.3 Not published Oracle JavaFX 21.0.13, 25.0.5, 27.0.1 Not published Java 17 is a long-term support release, so many banks, cloud services and back-end systems still run it. Version 17.0.6 shipped in January 2023, so the reported range covers almost four years of builds. Because OpenJDK is sold in many vendor builds, the fix may arrive on different dates under different version names. South Korean officials told teams to check the exact JVM, vendor, and build in use, including Java inside containers and apps. This is not the first Java scare this season. Oracle already issued an emergency Java update in October for CVE-2026-91403, a certificate trust bug rated 9.1. Our earlier report on Oracle’s 943-patch August update showed how fast these bundles are growing. Java apps are also under pressure elsewhere. Rapid7 reported exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 in Apache Axis, which affects Confluence Data Center. Start with a full list of Java runtimes, including those inside containers. Close any internet access that the business does not need. Test the November update in a staging system, then roll it out quickly. Keep backups ready in case an update fails. Oracle’s only advice so far is to apply the update as soon as possible, and no workaround exists for this CVE. Watch Oracle’s advisory, your OpenJDK vendor, and the CVE record for updates. Until a fix is confirmed for your build, treat every exposed Java 17 server as a priority. What Are Leading Organizations Doing About AI and Cyber Risks? Find Out. View Agenda!

items.title: Pre-orders open for Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard
items.summary: It’s time! Pre-orders are now open for Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard. We know a lot of you have been waiting for this (by far the largest email waitlist we’ve had on any product), and we’re excited to get it into your hands. A fully refundable $50 deposit is all you need to place your pre-order. The first batches ship in Q1 2027 to every region we serve, and we’re cranking up manufacturing capacity to get as many out as we can in that window. We wanted an excellent living room keyboard as much as you do, and we’ve spent all year perfecting it. We posted two videos today digging into what we’ve created. The first is a product overview talking through the core features and functionality. The second is a head to head comparison to the product we built this keyboard to replace. Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard is our take on what the ideal integrated keyboard and touchpad should be, for all the scenarios where a traditional keyboard and mouse don’t make sense. The living room is one obvious home for it, and it also makes a great setup keyboard for servers, single board computers, and sim rigs. We know many of you want to use it as your primary desk keyboard too. It’s slim and portable, but dense and rigid with a 0.8mm steel plate inside. It also looks super cool with the translucent black back cover letting you see the internals. To get a crisp and tactile typing feel, we used the keyboard module directly from Framework Laptop 12 that we developed with Lite-On. The touchpad uses a Precision Touchpad touch controller from PixArt, the same supplier we use for all of our laptops, and runs at 120Hz for smooth, low-latency cursor movement. The connectivity is strong, with an included USB-A Dongle that stores in the back of the keyboard pre-paired on Channel 1, plus three additional channels to pair Bluetooth devices. The keyboard has a wired mode over USB-C and supports 8kHz polling for higher responsiveness too. All of this means it's compatible with an extremely wide range of host devices, like Linux and Windows PCs, smartphones and tablets, BIOS menus, game consoles, Steam Machines, Raspberry Pis, smart TVs, and more. If you’re a Mac user, we developed what we believe is the best Mac compatibility of any non-Apple keyboard and touchpad. You can hold Fn + O for 3 seconds to switch any of the channels into Mac Mode (Fn + P for 3 seconds to switch back). We’re emulating not just the keyboard shortcuts, but also most of the macOS multi-finger touchpad gestures. We’ve spent the final stretch of our development time optimizing battery life to the fullest. For setup and living room use cases, standby battery life is especially important, since the keyboard may go months between uses, and you want it to work instantly when you next pick it up. In the lowest “on and connected” power state, the keyboard draws under 50 microamps from its 1200mAh battery. That means it will last for well over a year when used sporadically. It also lasts over a month with hours of use per day at a desk (note: battery life will always vary depending on your usage patterns), and you can recharge easily over USB-C. Since this is a Framework product, it’s designed to last in other ways too. The rechargeable battery is replaceable if you ever manage to wear through the cycle life. Continuing with our product philosophy, we’ve made large parts of this open for modification and extension. The firmware is an open source fork of ZMK (publishing to GitHub soon), and you can use the broad ecosystem of tools like ZMK Studio to remap keys. The Control Board that powers this keyboard has an ultra-low-power Nordic nRF54LM20A wireless microcontroller and a 0.1” header to enable expansion and re-use. We’re making it available on its own for developers to build their own custom keyboards around. We’ve also released open source surface CAD so you can design and 3D print accessories, like sim rig mounts. Alongside the keyboard, we designed a USB-A Adapter Expansion Card . This lets you fit the Dongle flush in a Framework Laptop or Desktop. It also works great with many USB-A dongles from other brands. This Expansion Card will be available in the Framework Marketplace early next year. The initial version of Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard has a US English ANSI layout. We’d love to hear what other languages you’d like, so please let us know through this survey . We’ve heard from a lot of businesses interested in this keyboard as well. If you’re looking at purchasing larger volumes, you can reach out to our Framework for Business team . We know that this keyboard will be the first Framework product that many of you own. It’s a simple, useful, long lasting, open keyboard in a category that really needed a better option. We can’t wait to see what you think of it! We have one other update today. The new 192GB configuration of Framework Desktop starts shipping this week. We opened pre-orders at the end of September and sold through the first batch much more quickly than we expected to. There is a lot of demand for being able to own your AI compute and run much larger models entirely under your control. Pre-orders are still open, with the current batch shipping before the end of the year. We anticipate memory pricing increasing further in 2027, so if you’re looking at Framework Desktop configurations in high memory capacities, you should consider getting in ahead of that.

items.title: Fix what matters, not what’s easy: why severity scores are failing security teams
items.summary: Most people who run an application security programme will recognise this. The backlog grows every quarter. The team works harder every quarter. The gap between what gets found and what gets fixed keeps getting wider anyway. This feeling now has numbers behind it. Black Duck’s 2027 AI Readiness Report analysed 65.5 million application security findings across roughly 13,100 applications at 533 organisations between June 2025 and May 2026. In June 2025, organisations were discovering 11 new findings for every one they closed. By May 2026 the ratio was 18 to 1, and it peaked at 22 to 1 in December. In April 2026 alone, 10.4 million unresolved findings were added to backlogs. By the end of the study, only about one finding in ten had been closed. The attacker’s clock has changed For most of the past decade, defenders had time on their side. In 2018, the mean time between a vulnerability’s disclosure and its first exploit was 2.6 years. According to the Zero Day Clock, it is now under a day. Frontier AI models are speeding this up further. Exploits that once took specialist skill and weeks of effort can now be produced quickly and cheaply. Remediation hasn’t moved at the same speed. At the median, findings from static analysis (SAST) closed in 28 days and open source findings from software composition analysis (SCA) in 39 days. Those are the fast ones. Findings from dynamic testing took 316 days, and findings from manual testing took 232. When exploitation runs on an hourly clock and remediation on a monthly one, every open finding is a window an attacker can use. Easiest first, most dangerous last The most uncomfortable finding is about order. If severity decided what got fixed first, critical vulnerabilities would close fastest. In the highest-volume testing methods, they don’t. Critical open source vulnerabilities took a median of 58 days to close, against 22 days for high-severity ones. In SAST, high-severity findings closed more slowly than medium or low. Some of that reflects harder fixes. A critical flaw in an open source component may need a major version upgrade, while a low-severity fix is often a simple patch. But the overall pattern is clear: when findings arrive by the million, teams fix what is easiest. Nothing deliberate is setting the order. Fixing criticals first would be an improvement, but severity alone isn’t the answer either. In the vulnerability advisories Black Duck’s researchers published in 2025, known exploits existed for 45% of high-severity vulnerabilities, 39% of medium-severity ones and 31% of low-severity ones. AI models can also chain lower-severity weaknesses into serious multistep attacks. A medium-severity flaw with a working exploit in a reachable part of a production application can be more urgent than a theoretical critical one. “Lower priority” can no longer mean “never”. Less public intelligence to lean on Prioritisation is also getting harder for another reason. In April 2026, NIST announced that it would prioritise enrichment for only a narrow subset of CVEs in the National Vulnerability Database. Most new disclosures will now arrive without the analysis that many programmes rely on, just as AI-driven discovery pushes disclosure volumes up. Teams that triage from NVD scores alone will need another source of vulnerability intelligence. What the faster teams do differently The data also shows that remediation speed tracks operational practice more closely than vulnerability volume. Organisations that ran SCA scans 10 to 29 times a month closed open source findings in an average of 30 days, against 66 days for those scanning less than monthly. That is a correlation, not a magic lever. Frequent scanning usually means testing is wired into pipelines, with findings routed straight to the developers who can fix them. The largest organisations in the dataset also show what deliberate prioritisation looks like. Those with more than 10,000 employees closed critical and high-severity findings in a median of 12 days, against 19 days for all findings. Several smaller bands showed the reverse, taking longer on their most serious issues than on everything else. Where to start For practitioners, the report points to a handful of practical steps: Check your own data. Are your critical findings actually closing before your low-severity ones? If not, find out why. Prioritise by exploitability, reachability and business context, not severity scores alone. Set timeframes for lower-severity findings too. Track three numbers together: median time to close, percentage of findings closed and the discovery-to-closure ratio. A fast median means little if only a fraction of findings ever gets fixed. Close coverage gaps. Two-thirds of applications in the dataset were tested with a single method, yet manual testing, the smallest source of findings, turned up critical or high-severity issues more than half the time. Automate what can be automated, such as dependency upgrades and validated code fixes, and keep people for the judgement calls. No amount of headcount will close a gap that grows by millions of findings a month. This is an operating-model problem, not a staffing one. The teams that keep up will be the ones that decide deliberately what to fix first, and then fix it before an attacker gets there.

Most people who run an application security programme will recognise this. The backlog grows every quarter. The team works harder every quarter. The gap between what gets found and what gets fixed keeps getting wider anyway.

This feeling now has numbers behind it. Black Duck’s 2027 AI Readiness Report analysed 65.5 million application security findings across roughly 13,100 applications at 533 organisations between June 2025 and May 2026. In June 2025, organisations were discovering 11 new findings for every one they closed. By May 2026 the ratio was 18 to 1, and it peaked at 22 to 1 in December. In April 2026 alone, 10.4 million unresolved findings were added to backlogs.

By the end of the study, only about one finding in ten had been closed.

The attacker’s clock has changed

For most of the past decade, defenders had time on their side. In 2018, the mean time between a vulnerability’s disclosure and its first exploit was 2.6 years. According to the Zero Day Clock, it is now under a day. Frontier AI models are speeding this up further. Exploits that once took specialist skill and weeks of effort can now be produced quickly and cheaply.

Remediation hasn’t moved at the same speed. At the median, findings from static analysis (SAST) closed in 28 days and open source findings from software composition analysis (SCA) in 39 days. Those are the fast ones. Findings from dynamic testing took 316 days, and findings from manual testing took 232. When exploitation runs on an hourly clock and remediation on a monthly one, every open finding is a window an attacker can use.

Easiest first, most dangerous last

The most uncomfortable finding is about order. If severity decided what got fixed first, critical vulnerabilities would close fastest. In the highest-volume testing methods, they don’t. Critical open source vulnerabilities took a median of 58 days to close, against 22 days for high-severity ones. In SAST, high-severity findings closed more slowly than medium or low.

Some of that reflects harder fixes. A critical flaw in an open source component may need a major version upgrade, while a low-severity fix is often a simple patch. But the overall pattern is clear: when findings arrive by the million, teams fix what is easiest. Nothing deliberate is setting the order.

Fixing criticals first would be an improvement, but severity alone isn’t the answer either. In the vulnerability advisories Black Duck’s researchers published in 2025, known exploits existed for 45% of high-severity vulnerabilities, 39% of medium-severity ones and 31% of low-severity ones. AI models can also chain lower-severity weaknesses into serious multistep attacks. A medium-severity flaw with a working exploit in a reachable part of a production application can be more urgent than a theoretical critical one. “Lower priority” can no longer mean “never”.

Less public intelligence to lean on

Prioritisation is also getting harder for another reason. In April 2026, NIST announced that it would prioritise enrichment for only a narrow subset of CVEs in the National Vulnerability Database. Most new disclosures will now arrive without the analysis that many programmes rely on, just as AI-driven discovery pushes disclosure volumes up. Teams that triage from NVD scores alone will need another source of vulnerability intelligence.

What the faster teams do differently

The data also shows that remediation speed tracks operational practice more closely than vulnerability volume. Organisations that ran SCA scans 10 to 29 times a month closed open source findings in an average of 30 days, against 66 days for those scanning less than monthly. That is a correlation, not a magic lever. Frequent scanning usually means testing is wired into pipelines, with findings routed straight to the developers who can fix them.

The largest organisations in the dataset also show what deliberate prioritisation looks like. Those with more than 10,000 employees closed critical and high-severity findings in a median of 12 days, against 19 days for all findings. Several smaller bands showed the reverse, taking longer on their most serious issues than on everything else.

Where to start

For practitioners, the report points to a handful of practical steps:

  • Check your own data. Are your critical findings actually closing before your low-severity ones? If not, find out why.
  • Prioritise by exploitability, reachability and business context, not severity scores alone. Set timeframes for lower-severity findings too.
  • Track three numbers together: median time to close, percentage of findings closed and the discovery-to-closure ratio. A fast median means little if only a fraction of findings ever gets fixed.
  • Close coverage gaps. Two-thirds of applications in the dataset were tested with a single method, yet manual testing, the smallest source of findings, turned up critical or high-severity issues more than half the time.
  • Automate what can be automated, such as dependency upgrades and validated code fixes, and keep people for the judgement calls.

No amount of headcount will close a gap that grows by millions of findings a month. This is an operating-model problem, not a staffing one. The teams that keep up will be the ones that decide deliberately what to fix first, and then fix it before an attacker gets there.

 

The post Fix what matters, not what’s easy: why severity scores are failing security teams appeared first on IT Security Guru.

Instead of stealing a password, an attacker persuades someone to approve a sign-in on a legitimate site simply by entering a code. The resulting access often can reach email, files, or other cloud services, depending on the account and the permissions granted. Microsoft worked hard with partners in industry and law enforcement to disrupt EvilTokens in September 2026. That led us to a different question: what else can an attacker do with a phished device code authorization? What happens when the same trick targets an AI agent rather than a mailbox? We used GitHub Copilot CLI as an illustrative example. Depending on its configuration, it can work with code, run commands on a user’s machine, retain context across sessions, and allow an active session to be steered remotely. Like many command-line tools, it supports the OAuth device flow for sign-in. The phishing technique itself is not specific to GitHub or Copilot CLI: any public client that supports the device flow can be abused the same way, and the attacker chooses the requested scopes when starting the flow. We explored this scenario in a controlled lab simulation. A victim test account approved a GitHub device-code request initiated by an attacker client we controlled. With that approval, we were able to analyze four possible outcomes: Steer an active Copilot CLI session remotely, if the user has enabled remote control and organization policy allows it, and, subject to local permissions and approval settings, have the agent run commands on the user’s machine. Add misleading entries to the agent’s memory that could influence later interactions. Read Copilot CLI sessions that were synchronized to the cloud. Access private repositories available to the affected account. These are proof-of-concept results showing how existing features, working as designed, could be abused after a phished authorization; they are not attacks we have observed in the wild. These outcomes require the victim user to approve a device code request initiated by the attacker; each outcome also depends on the account permissions and enabled features described below. Later in this post, we show how Microsoft Defender helps detect these attacks by connecting phishing attempts with GitHub authentication activity, and how organizations can disrupt suspicious access to protect affected identities. From a familiar phishing technique to an AI coding agent The OAuth device flow helps clients such as command-line tools sign in without displaying a full browser. A client requests a short code; the user enters it on the service’s verification page; the requesting client receives access after approval. In device code phishing, the attacker starts the request and persuades someone else to approve it. Microsoft has reported device code phishing against accounts in several campaigns, including Storm-2372 , an AI-enabled campaign in 2026, and EvilTokens . Those cases motivated us to examine a different target: a coding agent that can work with repositories and, when remote control is enabled, expose an active session to remote interaction. The remainder of this post describes a controlled GitHub Copilot CLI simulation; we have not observed the four outcomes below in those campaigns or in the wild. How the attack works Figure 1. A user approves a legitimate GitHub device-code request that was initiated by the attacker-controlled client. Conceptual illustration. Initiate: The attacker starts a device-code sign-in request. In our simulation, we used the Copilot CLI client, but any device-flow client could be used. Lure: The attacker sends the short code and GitHub verification link to the user, for example under the pretext of an IT request or a Copilot license check. The verification page is genuinely hosted by GitHub; the legitimate domain alone does not establish who initiated the request. Approve: The user opens the GitHub page, signs in if needed, and approves the request. This is the social engineering step. Sign in: After approval, the attacker-controlled client completes the sign-in automatically. Operate: The attacker can act within the permissions granted to the application and the resources available to the affected account. The request behind the code The following example shows the initial HTTP request to GitHub’s device authorization endpoint . The Copilot CLI client identifier is public; it is not a client secret. The attacker sends the short code returned by GitHub to the user. Once the user approves it, the requesting client signs in without another manual step. GitHub Device Code Authentication (Simplified) Endpoint: GitHub Device Authorization Endpoint Client ID: Requested scopes: The request looks legitimate The user signs in on the real GitHub site, not a lookalike page. A familiar domain therefore cannot tell the user whether the request was theirs. An authorization also appears under a legitimate application name; the name alone cannot distinguish the attacker-controlled client from an expected sign-in. One approval, four ways the impact can spread The device code approval was only the starting point. What an attacker could do next depended on the account’s permissions, enabled features, memory settings, and whether an active session could be controlled remotely. Figure 2. Four possible outcomes in the lab, each subject to the account’s permissions and enabled features. Conceptual illustration. 1. An attacker can steer an enabled remote session Copilot CLI supports remote steering of an active interactive session when the user has enabled remote control for that session and organization policy allows it. In our lab, the attacker-controlled client used the test account’s authorization to interact with a remotely controllable session. The agent ran a command on the test machine, subject to the session’s approval prompts and local operating-system permissions. This demonstrates misuse of an authorized remote-session capability working as designed; it is not unauthenticated remote code execution and does not apply when remote control is disabled, the session is not running, or the machine is offline. Figure 3. Remote-session misuse is bounded by the local machine’s permissions and approval controls. Conceptual illustration. 2. Memory can carry the attack forward Copilot Memory can retain repository facts and user preferences. In the simulation, we added misleading entries using the agent’s /memory command. If those entries are used in later interactions, the effects can outlast the initial sign-in. The behavior depends on which memory features and policies are enabled. Figure 4. Misleading memory can affect later agent interactions. Conceptual illustration. 3. Synced sessions reveal earlier context Where cloud session storage is enabled, we could read the test account’s synced Copilot CLI sessions, including sessions from before the simulation. They may contain code snippets, file paths, architecture discussions, and other work context. For Copilot Business and Enterprise, availability depends on the organization’s session-storage policy; syncing a session does not itself enable remote control. 4. Repository access follows the account In the lab, the authorization let us access private repositories available to the test account. The request included the repo scope along with read:user, read:org, gist, and codespace. These scopes are chosen by the client that starts the flow; the resulting repository access reflects the requested scopes and the account’s permissions, not a property of Copilot CLI itself. The potential exposure is bounded by the account’s repository access, which can include application code and infrastructure definitions. A phishing message, a click, and a GitHub authorization can each look unremarkable on their own. The challenge for defenders is recognizing when they belong to the same attempted takeover. The legitimate verification page is part of the story, not evidence that the request was safe. Turning a phishing attempt into a Defender signal Microsoft Defender helps organizations detect and respond to device code phishing targeting GitHub accounts. With the GitHub Enterprise Cloud connector enabled in Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, organizations gain visibility into GitHub activity that can support investigations of suspicious authorization patterns. As part of our research, we developed two detections for suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing, covering attacks delivered through email and Microsoft Teams. These detections correlate suspicious messages and clicks with subsequent GitHub OAuth token creation and regeneration events, helping identify potentially unauthorized Copilot CLI authorizations that might otherwise appear legitimate. Initial Access / Credential Access Microsoft Defender XDR: Suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing via Microsoft Teams Suspected device code phishing delivered through Microsoft Teams, potentially resulting in unauthorized GitHub Copilot CLI access Initial Access / Credential Access Beyond detection, we also developed a disruption action for GitHub Enterprise Managed Users (EMU). This action suspends the affected managed identity through the organization’s identity provider, interrupting the attacker’s access. We validated this capability in our research environment. Responders should also review and revoke unexpected OAuth authorizations, verify that access is blocked, and investigate potentially affected sessions, repositories, and saved memory. Together, these capabilities help security teams move from identifying a potential phishing attempt to containing the affected identity. Detection and disruption availability depend on the supported configuration, required telemetry, identity integration, and deployment prerequisites. Figure 5. Microsoft Defender alert generated for suspected GitHub Copilot CLI device code phishing via email. Figure 6. Research model for identifying and containing the affected managed identity. Conceptual illustration. Mitigation and protection guidance Make the approval rule clear to everyone who uses developer and AI tools: enter a device code only for a sign-in you initiated yourself. An unexpected request to “verify” GitHub or activate Copilot should be treated as a phishing attempt, even if the page is hosted on github.com. GitHub’s own verification page warns users never to use a code sent by someone else. These protections can help with malicious links and provide investigation context; a legitimate GitHub verification URL still requires the user to recognize an unsolicited code request. Review GitHub Copilot CLI session settings . For organization-provided seats, GitHub’s “Store local sessions in the Cloud” policy determines whether sessions can be stored and remotely controlled. Choose the least permissive setting that supports your workflows. Remote control also requires an active, online interactive session. Review authorized OAuth applications in GitHub account settings and revoke authorizations that are unexpected or no longer needed. Limit repository access with appropriate organization roles so an affected account cannot reach more code than its work requires. If Copilot Memory is enabled, use GitHub’s memory-management controls to review and remove suspicious repository facts or user preferences. Disabling memory does not automatically delete entries already stored, so review the saved content during incident response. Connect GitHub Enterprise Cloud to Defender for Cloud Apps and validate the activity available in your environment before relying on it for investigations. Remember: A legitimate sign-in can still be the wrong one The most striking part of this simulation was how little needed to look suspicious. The user visited the real GitHub site and approved a normal-looking request. Yet the approval belonged to a client the user had not started. From there, the consequences depended on what that identity could access and which Copilot CLI capabilities were enabled. That is why this is more than a story about a code. Ultimately, protecting against device code phishing requires both user awareness and the ability to connect suspicious authorization activity to the phishing attempt that preceded it. items.title: Hackers Abuse Microsoft SharePoint and GitHub to Hide GraphDoor Backdoor Attacks on Government Networks
items.summary: Hackers are hiding a backdoor named GraphDoor inside normal Microsoft and Ably traffic. The goal is to spy on government networks in Asia and Africa. Kaspersky’s GReAT team detailed the findings on November 17, 2026, in the second part of its Operation ShadowCloud research. The report also lists the plug-ins GraphDoor loads and points to Chinese-speaking threat groups as possible owners of the tools. GraphDoor first opens a named pipe built from its own process ID, in the form \\.\pipe\p%lu . Later plug-ins write their results to this pipe. The malware then creates an Intel_Log folder inside ProgramData, with a random GUID folder inside it. Next, it collects system details. These include the network adapter, Windows version, public and private IP addresses, user name, host name, and a list of running processes. To hide its Windows API calls, it hashes function names with the DJB2 method. It also uses a vectored exception handler, which forces an error on purpose so that a small routine runs the target call. The data is then encrypted with AES, Base64 encoded, and sent out. GraphDoor SharePoint Backdoor GraphDoor does not use a normal command server. It connects to login.microsoftonline.com and signs in as a malicious app, not as a person, using a client ID and secret stored inside the malware. That sign-in returns a token for the Microsoft Graph API. With that token, the malware uploads the stolen host data to a SharePoint document library. The file is named main. .js.map , which makes it look like a harmless JavaScript source map. The victim code is a random eight-character string. Researchers saw the SharePoint site buildersemp.sharepoint[.]com used for this. A second site, cskautogo[.]sharepoint[.]com , is also listed in the report. The malware then asks SharePoint lists for three plug-ins. They are scr.ts for screenshots, pr.ts for process lists, and kl.ts for key logging. It only fetches the keylogger if a file named log.lock already exists on the machine. After that, it checks the same lists for command files that start with its own victim code and end in .js , .swp , .tmp , .kmap , .pmap , or .apmap . This design is not new. Cisco Talos found a similar Rust backdoor named Antino, which uses Outlook and OneDrive for control, as Cyber Security News reported . In both cases, defenders see only calls to a trusted Microsoft service. GraphDoor supports the same commands as its sibling, GitDoor, and adds two more. The shell command runs text through cmd.exe /C . The adsmload command hides payloads as fake MAC addresses inside Base64 text, then turns them back into bytes with the Windows call RtlEthernetStringToAddressA . Each plug-in is a small loader followed by a COFF object, with an entry point named go . The keylogger saves keystrokes and mouse clicks to %APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat , locked with a random XOR key. The screenshot plug-in sends JPEG images through the pipe. The process plug-in turns on the SeDebugPrivilege right before it lists running programs. A moveDir.ts plug-in copies the backdoor files to a new folder and can delete the old copies. Three proxy plug-ins give the actors a path into the network. One is a patched copy of the open-source reverse proxy Erfrp, and it reads its settings from shared memory instead of a file. Another uses the Ably real-time messaging service through its official Go SDK. The third is a SOCKS5 proxy that moves TCP traffic over Ably’s Pusher-compatible WebSocket endpoint. Because the C2 host name comes through these proxy plug-ins or through an Ably channel, the backdoor holds no fixed C2 domain. Defenders cannot simply pull a domain out of the sample and block it. Sophos also saw ably[.]net and ably[.]io in a separate China-linked case, which Cyber Security News covered here . Kaspersky says it cannot yet name one group. Still, GitDoor files appeared in the same folders as tools from FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle, within one day of each other. In one case, a renamed Avast file called excint.exe loaded a bad wtsapi32.dll on March 6, 2026, and GitDoor files landed in the same folder on March 5. The DLL used the RC4 key iotrh^%4CFGTj , which ESET has tied to FamousSparrow . In the CopperTurtle case, pdfset.exe in the PDF24 folder loaded the PLEAD RAT on May 3, 2026, and GitDoor followed on May 4. Kaspersky says this does not prove a direct link. Cyber Security News also covered FamousSparrow’s newer Exchange intrusions , which show how active that group still is. Two IP addresses, 103[.]106[.]230[.]33 and 123[.]58[.]205[.]105 , resolve to ms[.]twnic[.]top and ekmt[.]tw . Both domains also served as Cobalt Strike beacon servers on machines infected with GraphDoor. The report lists many more proxy server IPs for defenders to check. Kaspersky notes that calls to Microsoft Graph, GitHub, and Ably look like normal business traffic, so network tools often miss them. Teams should watch for odd app sign-ins in Entra ID, unknown SharePoint sites, and files with names like .js.map in document libraries. They should also treat any new remote tool, such as MeshCentral Agent, as suspicious. Defenders should also hunt for sideloaded DLLs in folders such as PDF24 and ProgramData\excint . The report’s hashes, domains, and IPs can be added to blocklists. items.title: Hackers Exploit Unpatched Microsoft Exchange Servers to Deploy Custom RATs Across Southeast Asia
items.summary: Hackers are exploiting unpatched Microsoft Exchange servers and vulnerable web servers to break into government networks across Southeast Asia, deploying custom remote access trojans built for quiet, long-term spying. The campaign combines server exploitation, targeted phishing, credential theft, and mailbox access to pursue sensitive government information. The activity has targeted government entities since at least July 2025. Investigators observed attackers deploying PerfectPioneer RAT before introducing its modular successor, KUKURAT, in March 2026. The operation focused on maintaining access and collecting intelligence, with targeted filenames suggesting an interest in international relations and internal political affairs. Researchers from Unit 42 identified both previously undocumented malware families and tracked the campaign as TGR-STA-0049, also known as REF7707, Earth Alux, and Ink Dragon. The investigation shows how the attackers steadily updated their tools while combining familiar intrusion methods with newer ways to hide network traffic and endpoint activity. Hackers Exploit Unpatched Microsoft Exchange Servers Server exploitation was the primary entry method. Attackers compromised vulnerable Exchange and web servers, planted web shells, and used that access to run reconnaissance commands and deploy malware. The report does not identify the specific Exchange vulnerabilities exploited, so the intrusions should not be attributed to a particular CVE or exploit chain. The approach echoes earlier Exchange server backdoor attacks involving other threat groups, although those incidents do not establish a connection to this campaign. Execution of the PerfectPioneer RAT from a web shell, as shown in Cortex XDR (Source – Unit42) Here, researchers observed a mixture of custom and publicly available web shells, including ASPXSpy, Godzilla, and Suo5 variants. Phishing provided a second route into targeted systems. Attackers used lookalike government domains and executable files disguised with PDF icons. Opening these files launched malware alongside a decoy document. One lure impersonated an official Myanmar election notice, while another delivery method ran a genuine GlobalProtect installer as malware executed in the background. PerfectPioneer is written in Go, and researchers recovered six variants. The most complete version supports file transfers, shell commands, process management, screenshots, keylogging, code injection, and SOCKS5 proxying. Some variants also contain an operator safety mechanism that blocks destructive or conspicuous commands, reducing the chance that an attacker’s mistake exposes the intrusion. Both malware families support HTTP/3 communications over QUIC, which uses UDP rather than TCP. This matters because some network defenses inspect TCP traffic more closely than UDP traffic. PerfectPioneer’s analyzed communication framework can fall back to HTTP/2, while KUKURAT has separate HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 variants. Blocking QUIC alone therefore does not remove the threat. KUKURAT Hides Activity While Attackers Steal Credentials and Email KUKURAT shifts most capabilities into separate DLL modules retrieved from the command server when needed. Written in C++, its code supports at least 12 named modules covering functions such as screenshots, keylogging, file management, scanning, remote execution, and lateral movement. This separates the small core agent from much of its operational functionality. Unlike the distinct TinyRCT government espionage campaign , this operation also features a coordinated camouflage engine. KUKURAT can generate harmless-looking web requests, imitate browser-related registry activity, and rapidly create and delete temporary files. Code snippet from the PerfectPioneer RAT’s isDangerousCommand code (Source – Unit42) These actions aim to bury meaningful signals among artificial noise rather than simply conceal a single malicious file. Attackers also deployed a watchdog component that could restart KUKURAT after it stopped responding. After compromising domain controllers, they modified domain log-on scripts so legitimate user authentication triggered malware downloads and execution on additional endpoints. Researchers also observed the use of established remote administration methods for movement inside compromised networks. Credential theft included LSASS memory dumping, DCSync, Mimikatz, ProcDump, and SharpDPAPI. The attackers then examined Exchange impersonation rights and, in observed cases, granted a compromised account broad mailbox access. Their document collection targeted office files, PDFs, and images, linking endpoint compromise directly to the campaign’s intelligence-gathering objective. The pattern reinforces lessons from other Exchange server exploitation campaigns without implying shared attribution. Defenders should patch exposed servers, investigate existing compromises, audit domain log-on scripts, and review Exchange permissions. Unit 42 additionally recommends inspecting or restricting QUIC traffic and monitoring suspicious credential-dumping behavior. Removing malware without addressing stolen credentials, mailbox permissions, and domain persistence may leave attackers with routes back into the environment. items.summary_html:
Hackers are exploiting unpatched Microsoft Exchange servers and vulnerable web servers to break into government networks across Southeast Asia, deploying custom remote access trojans built for quiet, long-term spying.

The campaign combines server exploitation, targeted phishing, credential theft, and mailbox access to pursue sensitive government information.

The activity has targeted government entities since at least July 2025. Investigators observed attackers deploying PerfectPioneer RAT before introducing its modular successor, KUKURAT, in March 2026.

The operation focused on maintaining access and collecting intelligence, with targeted filenames suggesting an interest in international relations and internal political affairs.

Researchers from Unit 42 identified both previously undocumented malware families and tracked the campaign as TGR-STA-0049, also known as REF7707, Earth Alux, and Ink Dragon.

The investigation shows how the attackers steadily updated their tools while combining familiar intrusion methods with newer ways to hide network traffic and endpoint activity.

Hackers Exploit Unpatched Microsoft Exchange Servers

Server exploitation was the primary entry method. Attackers compromised vulnerable Exchange and web servers, planted web shells, and used that access to run reconnaissance commands and deploy malware.

The report does not identify the specific Exchange vulnerabilities exploited, so the intrusions should not be attributed to a particular CVE or exploit chain.

The approach echoes earlier Exchange server backdoor attacks involving other threat groups, although those incidents do not establish a connection to this campaign.

Execution of the PerfectPioneer RAT from a web shell, as shown in Cortex XDR (Source – Unit42)

Here, researchers observed a mixture of custom and publicly available web shells, including ASPXSpy, Godzilla, and Suo5 variants. Phishing provided a second route into targeted systems.

Attackers used lookalike government domains and executable files disguised with PDF icons. Opening these files launched malware alongside a decoy document.

One lure impersonated an official Myanmar election notice, while another delivery method ran a genuine GlobalProtect installer as malware executed in the background.

PerfectPioneer is written in Go, and researchers recovered six variants. The most complete version supports file transfers, shell commands, process management, screenshots, keylogging, code injection, and SOCKS5 proxying.

Some variants also contain an operator safety mechanism that blocks destructive or conspicuous commands, reducing the chance that an attacker’s mistake exposes the intrusion.

Both malware families support HTTP/3 communications over QUIC, which uses UDP rather than TCP. This matters because some network defenses inspect TCP traffic more closely than UDP traffic.

PerfectPioneer’s analyzed communication framework can fall back to HTTP/2, while KUKURAT has separate HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 variants. Blocking QUIC alone therefore does not remove the threat.

KUKURAT Hides Activity While Attackers Steal Credentials and Email

KUKURAT shifts most capabilities into separate DLL modules retrieved from the command server when needed. Written in C++, its code supports at least 12 named modules covering functions such as screenshots, keylogging, file management, scanning, remote execution, and lateral movement. This separates the small core agent from much of its operational functionality.

Unlike the distinct TinyRCT government espionage campaign, this operation also features a coordinated camouflage engine. KUKURAT can generate harmless-looking web requests, imitate browser-related registry activity, and rapidly create and delete temporary files.

Code snippet from the PerfectPioneer RAT’s isDangerousCommand code (Source – Unit42)

These actions aim to bury meaningful signals among artificial noise rather than simply conceal a single malicious file. Attackers also deployed a watchdog component that could restart KUKURAT after it stopped responding.

After compromising domain controllers, they modified domain log-on scripts so legitimate user authentication triggered malware downloads and execution on additional endpoints. Researchers also observed the use of established remote administration methods for movement inside compromised networks.

Credential theft included LSASS memory dumping, DCSync, Mimikatz, ProcDump, and SharpDPAPI. The attackers then examined Exchange impersonation rights and, in observed cases, granted a compromised account broad mailbox access.

Their document collection targeted office files, PDFs, and images, linking endpoint compromise directly to the campaign’s intelligence-gathering objective.

The pattern reinforces lessons from other Exchange server exploitation campaigns without implying shared attribution. Defenders should patch exposed servers, investigate existing compromises, audit domain log-on scripts, and review Exchange permissions.

Unit 42 additionally recommends inspecting or restricting QUIC traffic and monitoring suspicious credential-dumping behavior.

Removing malware without addressing stolen credentials, mailbox permissions, and domain persistence may leave attackers with routes back into the environment.

items.title: Autonomous Cyberattacks: New Trends and How to Prepare for It
items.summary: For years, “AI-powered attacks” meant better phishing emails. That era is over. In late 2025, Anthropic disclosed a state-sponsored espionage campaign in which an AI agent ran an estimated 80–90% of the tactical work against roughly 30 targets, with humans stepping in only at a handful of decision points. The attacker’s bottleneck is no longer headcount. It is tokens. For SOC analysts and detection engineers, this changes the math. Dwell time shrinks, attack volume scales with compute, and the TTPs we write rules for start to mutate on every run. Here is what autonomous attacks look like under the hood, and how to build a defense that moves at the same speed. Get Started For Free What are Autonomous AI Cyberattacks? An autonomous AI cyberattack is an intrusion where an AI agent plans, executes, and adapts the attack chain with minimal human direction. The operator sets an objective (“get domain admin at target X”) and the agent decides how to get there. The key difference from classic automation is reasoning. A script runs the same playbook every time. An agent reads tool output, notices a failed exploit, and tries another path. Think of it as moving from a loaded gun to a junior red teamer that never sleeps, works hundreds of targets in parallel, and costs a few dollars per hour of API time. How does Autonomous Attack work? Most autonomous attack frameworks run a simple loop: observe, plan, act, evaluate, repeat. An orchestrator model breaks the objective into small tasks and hands them to sub-agents wired to real tooling through frameworks like the Model Context Protocol (MCP): scanners, credential dumpers, browsers, shells. A typical run maps cleanly to MITRE ATT&CK: Reconnaissance (TA0043): the agent enumerates exposed services, scrapes employee data, and ranks targets by value. Initial Access (TA0001): it writes or adapts an exploit for a discovered weakness, tests it, and retries on failure. Credential Access and Lateral Movement (TA0006, TA0008): it harvests secrets, validates them, and pivots, logging every step for the operator. Collection and Exfiltration (TA0009, TA0010): it sorts stolen data by intelligence value before sending it out. The trick that makes this work is task decomposition. Each sub-task looks benign in isolation (“scan this host,” “test this login”), which is exactly how attackers have slipped past model safeguards. The defensive takeaway: the signal lives in the sequence and the tempo, not in any single event. How to defend against Autonomous AI Attacks? Agents are fast, but they are not subtle. They generate request rates no human operator could sustain, retry aggressively, and sometimes hallucinate credentials or findings. That noise is your advantage. Focus detection on: Behavior over indicators. IOCs from an agent-driven campaign may be unique per run. Write Sigma rules around behaviors such as rapid sequential discovery commands, burst authentication attempts across many accounts, or a new process spawning dozens of recon tools in seconds. Velocity and correlation. Chain low-severity events into high-confidence alerts. Ten benign actions within 60 seconds from one identity is a story worth telling. Identity and API telemetry. Agents live on tokens and service accounts. Monitor anomalous API usage, impossible-speed sessions, and unexpected calls to LLM endpoints from servers. Deception. Honeytokens and decoy credentials work beautifully against agents that greedily validate everything they find. How are LLMs used in Autonomous Attacks? LLMs play three roles in the modern attack stack: The brain. Commercial or open-weight models act as orchestrators, reasoning about what to do next and generating code on demand. The payload. Malware now queries models at runtime. CERT-UA’s LameHug, linked to APT28, used a hosted LLM to generate recon commands on the fly, and the PromptLock proof of concept showed ransomware writing its own Lua scripts via a locally run model. No static command strings means fewer signatures to match. The social engineer. Personalized phishing, voice cloning, and deepfake video now scale to thousands of targets at near-zero marginal cost. For detection engineers, this creates new telemetry worth hunting: outbound traffic to LLM APIs from non-user hosts, embedded API keys in binaries, local inference runtimes appearing on endpoints, and scripts that look freshly generated rather than copied from a known toolkit. How to prepare your business for such attacks? Preparation starts with an honest question: if an attacker could try every technique in your threat model tonight, in parallel, which ones would you catch? Map coverage to ATT&CK. Identify gaps against the techniques agents favor: discovery, credential access, and lateral movement. Prioritize by your real log sources, not a theoretical matrix. Shrink the exposed surface. Agents excel at finding forgotten assets. Continuous external attack surface management and fast patching of internet-facing systems remove their easiest wins. Harden identity. Enforce phishing-resistant MFA, rotate secrets, and kill standing privileges. Stolen credentials are fuel for every autonomous chain. Govern your own AI. Inventory internal agents, MCP servers, and LLM integrations. Every tool you give your own AI is a tool an attacker can hijack through prompt injection. Rehearse at machine speed. Run purple-team exercises with AI-assisted adversary emulation and measure time-to-detect in minutes, not days. How to Transform Security to Autonomous Defense? You cannot fight an agent with a ticket queue. Autonomous defense means letting machines handle the repetitive loop while analysts own judgment and strategy. In practice, that looks like: Detection-as-code pipelines. Rules live in version control, are tested automatically, and deploy to every SIEM, EDR, and data lake in minutes. Sigma as a vendor-agnostic format makes this portable. AI-assisted detection engineering. Use AI to translate threat reports into rules, convert queries across platforms, and tune noisy content. SOC Prime’s Uncoder AI does exactly this, turning CTI into ready-to-deploy detections and translating rules across dozens of SIEM, EDR, and data lake languages. Continuous content refresh. New behaviors appear weekly. Threat Detection Marketplace on the SOC Prime Platform delivers curated, ATT&CK-mapped rules as emerging threats surface, so coverage evolves without waiting on a backlog. Agentic triage with guardrails. Let AI agents enrich alerts, correlate context, and draft response actions, but keep humans approving anything destructive. Autonomy without oversight just gives the attacker a new target. The goal is not to replace analysts. It is to compress the detect-to-respond cycle so your team works on the 5% of cases that actually need a human brain. What are cybersecurity trends for Autonomous Attacks? Exploit windows collapse. AI systems already find real vulnerabilities at scale, as DARPA’s AI Cyber Challenge showed. Expect time from disclosure to weaponization to drop from weeks to hours. Runtime-generated malware goes mainstream. LLM-querying payloads will push defenders further toward behavioral detection. AI infrastructure becomes the target. Prompt injection, poisoned MCP servers, and hijacked agents will join the attack surface. Defense goes agent-versus-agent. SOCs that pair human expertise with AI-driven detection engineering will keep pace. Those that don’t will be outrun. The attackers have automated. Now it’s your turn. Explore the SOC Prime Platform to get behavior-based detections for emerging AI-driven threats into your stack today.
