For years, “AI-powered attacks” meant better phishing emails. That era is over. In late 2025, Anthropic disclosed a state-sponsored espionage campaign in which an AI agent ran an estimated 80–90% of the tactical work against roughly 30 targets, with humans stepping in only at a handful of decision points. The attacker’s bottleneck is no longer headcount. It is tokens.

For SOC analysts and detection engineers, this changes the math. Dwell time shrinks, attack volume scales with compute, and the TTPs we write rules for start to mutate on every run. Here is what autonomous attacks look like under the hood, and how to build a defense that moves at the same speed.

Get Started For Free

What are Autonomous AI Cyberattacks?

An autonomous AI cyberattack is an intrusion where an AI agent plans, executes, and adapts the attack chain with minimal human direction. The operator sets an objective (“get domain admin at target X”) and the agent decides how to get there.

The key difference from classic automation is reasoning. A script runs the same playbook every time. An agent reads tool output, notices a failed exploit, and tries another path. Think of it as moving from a loaded gun to a junior red teamer that never sleeps, works hundreds of targets in parallel, and costs a few dollars per hour of API time.

How does Autonomous Attack work?

Most autonomous attack frameworks run a simple loop: observe, plan, act, evaluate, repeat. An orchestrator model breaks the objective into small tasks and hands them to sub-agents wired to real tooling through frameworks like the Model Context Protocol (MCP): scanners, credential dumpers, browsers, shells.

A typical run maps cleanly to MITRE ATT&CK:

  1. Reconnaissance (TA0043): the agent enumerates exposed services, scrapes employee data, and ranks targets by value.
  2. Initial Access (TA0001): it writes or adapts an exploit for a discovered weakness, tests it, and retries on failure.
  3. Credential Access and Lateral Movement (TA0006, TA0008): it harvests secrets, validates them, and pivots, logging every step for the operator.
  4. Collection and Exfiltration (TA0009, TA0010): it sorts stolen data by intelligence value before sending it out.

The trick that makes this work is task decomposition. Each sub-task looks benign in isolation (“scan this host,” “test this login”), which is exactly how attackers have slipped past model safeguards. The defensive takeaway: the signal lives in the sequence and the tempo, not in any single event.

How to defend against Autonomous AI Attacks?

Agents are fast, but they are not subtle. They generate request rates no human operator could sustain, retry aggressively, and sometimes hallucinate credentials or findings. That noise is your advantage. Focus detection on:

  • Behavior over indicators. IOCs from an agent-driven campaign may be unique per run. Write Sigma rules around behaviors such as rapid sequential discovery commands, burst authentication attempts across many accounts, or a new process spawning dozens of recon tools in seconds.
  • Velocity and correlation. Chain low-severity events into high-confidence alerts. Ten benign actions within 60 seconds from one identity is a story worth telling.
  • Identity and API telemetry. Agents live on tokens and service accounts. Monitor anomalous API usage, impossible-speed sessions, and unexpected calls to LLM endpoints from servers.
  • Deception. Honeytokens and decoy credentials work beautifully against agents that greedily validate everything they find.
How are LLMs used in Autonomous Attacks?

LLMs play three roles in the modern attack stack:

  • The brain. Commercial or open-weight models act as orchestrators, reasoning about what to do next and generating code on demand.
  • The payload. Malware now queries models at runtime. CERT-UA’s LameHug, linked to APT28, used a hosted LLM to generate recon commands on the fly, and the PromptLock proof of concept showed ransomware writing its own Lua scripts via a locally run model. No static command strings means fewer signatures to match.
  • The social engineer. Personalized phishing, voice cloning, and deepfake video now scale to thousands of targets at near-zero marginal cost.

For detection engineers, this creates new telemetry worth hunting: outbound traffic to LLM APIs from non-user hosts, embedded API keys in binaries, local inference runtimes appearing on endpoints, and scripts that look freshly generated rather than copied from a known toolkit.

How to prepare your business for such attacks?

Preparation starts with an honest question: if an attacker could try every technique in your threat model tonight, in parallel, which ones would you catch?

  1. Map coverage to ATT&CK. Identify gaps against the techniques agents favor: discovery, credential access, and lateral movement. Prioritize by your real log sources, not a theoretical matrix.
  2. Shrink the exposed surface. Agents excel at finding forgotten assets. Continuous external attack surface management and fast patching of internet-facing systems remove their easiest wins.
  3. Harden identity. Enforce phishing-resistant MFA, rotate secrets, and kill standing privileges. Stolen credentials are fuel for every autonomous chain.
  4. Govern your own AI. Inventory internal agents, MCP servers, and LLM integrations. Every tool you give your own AI is a tool an attacker can hijack through prompt injection.
  5. Rehearse at machine speed. Run purple-team exercises with AI-assisted adversary emulation and measure time-to-detect in minutes, not days.
How to Transform Security to Autonomous Defense?

You cannot fight an agent with a ticket queue. Autonomous defense means letting machines handle the repetitive loop while analysts own judgment and strategy. In practice, that looks like:

  • Detection-as-code pipelines. Rules live in version control, are tested automatically, and deploy to every SIEM, EDR, and data lake in minutes. Sigma as a vendor-agnostic format makes this portable.
  • AI-assisted detection engineering. Use AI to translate threat reports into rules, convert queries across platforms, and tune noisy content. SOC Prime’s Uncoder AI does exactly this, turning CTI into ready-to-deploy detections and translating rules across dozens of SIEM, EDR, and data lake languages.
  • Continuous content refresh. New behaviors appear weekly. Threat Detection Marketplace on the SOC Prime Platform delivers curated, ATT&CK-mapped rules as emerging threats surface, so coverage evolves without waiting on a backlog.
  • Agentic triage with guardrails. Let AI agents enrich alerts, correlate context, and draft response actions, but keep humans approving anything destructive. Autonomy without oversight just gives the attacker a new target.

The goal is not to replace analysts. It is to compress the detect-to-respond cycle so your team works on the 5% of cases that actually need a human brain.

What are cybersecurity trends for Autonomous Attacks?
  • Exploit windows collapse. AI systems already find real vulnerabilities at scale, as DARPA’s AI Cyber Challenge showed. Expect time from disclosure to weaponization to drop from weeks to hours.
  • Runtime-generated malware goes mainstream. LLM-querying payloads will push defenders further toward behavioral detection.
  • AI infrastructure becomes the target. Prompt injection, poisoned MCP servers, and hijacked agents will join the attack surface.
  • Defense goes agent-versus-agent. SOCs that pair human expertise with AI-driven detection engineering will keep pace. Those that don’t will be outrun.

Hackers Use Fake Shipment ZIP Files and DLL Side-Loading to Deploy PureLogs and PureRAT Malware
items.summary: Hackers are using a shipment-themed ZIP archive to launch a Windows malware chain that combines a legitimate signed application, DLL side-loading, and hidden Python code. The attack disguises its components as shipping material, images, documents, and a browser updater before running a payload linked to PureLogs and PureRAT infrastructure. The case shows why a trusted digital signature does not make an entire software package safe. Here, the genuine application acts as the starting point, while a malicious library beside it drives execution. Similar business email malware campaigns have used delivery complaints and download lures to distribute these malware families, although the supplied findings do not establish a connection between those operations. Researchers from Unit 42, Shazan Khaja and Muhammet Algan, documented the activity in research dated November 16, 2026. They observed the infection chain on October 21 after a user downloaded the shipment-themed archive. Their findings trace execution from the extracted files to a decoded Windows payload communicating with infrastructure attributed to PureLogs and PureRAT campaigns. Hackers Use Fake Shipment ZIP Files and DLL Side-Loading Inside the archive, attackers placed a legitimate, validly signed, 32-bit Kingsoft PDF executable renamed to match the shipment lure. A malicious DLL sat alongside it. When the user launched the executable, Windows loaded that nearby library, handing control to attacker-supplied code without requiring changes to the signed program itself. The sequence unfolded within seconds. Windows Explorer wrote the DLL to disk at 03:02:53 UTC, consistent with archive extraction. The renamed application started at 03:03:06 and loaded the malicious library roughly one second later. Archive extraction for the next stage began at 03:03:09, showing how quickly execution followed the user’s action. This approach resembles other trusted application side-loading attacks in which genuine software loads a hostile neighboring library. However, the Kingsoft executable’s signature and hash are not evidence of infection on their own. Investigators need to examine its location, loaded libraries, and child processes rather than treating every copy as malicious. A downloaded ZIP archive disguised as a report uses DLL side-loading to decode and run a malicious Python script for #PureLogs / #PureRAT . Details at https://t.co/asDQbpBRpH pic.twitter.com/1pZw87RdpJ — Unit 42 (@Unit42_Intel) November 16, 2026 The DLL launched a command sequence that opened a decoy PDF while preparing the hidden payload. A signed WinRAR command-line program, disguised with an image extension, extracted a password-protected archive into the public user directory. The extracted package contained a Python runtime renamed to resemble Microsoft’s Edge updater. Several internal filenames used Korean-language phrases about chicken deliveries and refrigerator stock, unrelated to the shipment story. These strings help describe the package, but they do not establish the attackers’ identity or the victims’ location. The supplied research does not identify a threat actor or explain how the download link reached the user. Disguised Python Loader Decodes the Final Payload The renamed Python interpreter executed a one-line command that read another apparent PDF as raw bytes. Instead of displaying a document, it applied a repeating XOR key to recover Python code and passed that result to exec() . The document extension therefore concealed an encoded script rather than readable shipment information. The recovered script used randomized names and arithmetic expressions involving XOR, shifts, and addition to obscure its contents. It then decoded a large Base64 blob and applied another repeating XOR operation, producing a Windows Portable Executable file with an MZ header. These layers separated the visible lure from the final executable payload. Earlier reporting on Python DLL side-loading techniques provides context for this combination of trusted software and script execution. In this case, the decoded payload contacted the infrastructure listed below over TLSv1 on port 443. Unit 42’s findings associate that infrastructure with PureLogs and PureRAT campaigns, rather than independently proving that both families executed on the observed endpoint. For defenders, the strongest leads are behavioral: a signed application running from Downloads and loading a neighboring DLL, followed by command-shell activity, disguised archive extraction, and Python execution from a public directory. A Python command that decodes an apparent document and immediately executes its contents is another important investigation lead. items.title: ARTEX Detection: Hunting the AI Pentest Framework Turned Attack Platform
items.summary: Offensive AI is no longer a slide in a threat-landscape deck. It is sitting on attacker servers, wired to multiple LLM APIs, and probing production APIs at machine speed. ARTEX, an open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework developed in China, is the clearest example so far: a red-team tool that threat actors have adopted to automate reconnaissance, vulnerability probing, and exploitation end to end. For SOC analysts and detection engineers, ARTEX detection is a new kind of problem. There is no single malware family to fingerprint. Instead, you face an LLM-driven operator that adapts payloads, rotates techniques, and generates traffic volumes no human pentester could. This article walks through the ARTEX analysis available so far, the behaviors worth alerting on, and how to detect ARTEX across web, endpoint, and Linux telemetry. Get Started For Free ARTEX Analysis ARTEX went public on GitHub as Autumn-27/ARTEX on July 26, 2026, under AGPL-3.0. It is written in Go, runs a Next.js console on PostgreSQL, and sits on top of ScopeSentry, the same author’s asset-discovery platform ( Censys ). The architecture explains the telemetry you will see. A Planner agent turns an operator goal, such as “gain admin panel access,” into attack intents. Worker agents claim those intents, run tools like nmap, and write results back into an asset graph and an exploration graph. The loop repeats until the goal is met, using Anthropic, OpenAI, or any OpenAI-compatible model endpoint. That loop is fast. Mandiant and GTIG recorded 27 events within 23 seconds, plus automated error correction used to land webshells, as covered in our report on how ARTEX leads a new wave of agentic offensive frameworks alongside PentAGI and CAIRN. The author disowned malicious use on October 8 and took the repository down, but forks and rebrands such as ScopeWeaver still circulate. As of early November, Censys counted 1,465 exposed ARTEX consoles, most on default port 8787. Reported Campaign What ARTEX affects Nov 9, 2026 Storm-3358 targets financial organizations SSRF and anonymous file uploads, then WISP, vshell, and AdaptixC2 RATs plus cloud identity abuse Oct 27, 2026 Storm-0940 hits IT and software vendors Okta, Entra ID, and Cognito auth probing; account recovery abuse; IP and user-agent rotation Oct 21, 2026 ARTEX found on servers attacking Japanese companies API probing and WAF evasion in Japan and South Korea, driven by DeepSeek, Zhipu AI, and xAI models Oct 21, 2026 Storm-0940 ConnectWise supply-chain compromise (Microsoft) Sign-ins against 2,250+ tenants, peaking at 2,900 attempts per minute Oct 7, 2026 South Korean banks (CrowdStrike) A broker-facing loan service and an employee mobile system breached, data exfiltrated Detect ARTEX Detect ARTEX by behavior, not by name. Binaries get renamed and consoles get rebranded, but the explore-decide-execute loop leaves volumetric and sequential fingerprints across five log sources. Web server: 40x response spikes from a single IP, path traversal, file inclusion, and OS command injection patterns, and scripted files dropped into web directories. Wiz saw a fetch of /swagger/?format=openapi followed immediately by a random nonexistent URI, a clean mapping signature. Identity: failed-login bursts and access-denied spikes on Okta, Entra ID, and Cognito, password spraying, and abuse of account recovery workflows. Endpoint and Linux: web service accounts spawning shells, SSH known_hosts discovery, nmap, curl, or wget from unexpected parents, and netcat paired with RAT binaries. Cloud: an Azure write-then-delete of a throwaway blob, and AWS EC2 calls with –dry-run that test IAM permissions without changing state. Network: HTTP C2 to direct IPs on uncommon ports, and egress to LLM resellers or self-hosted proxies such as CLIProxyAPI and New API. ARTEX IOCs worth loading now include the ARTEX host 38.244.50[.]120 and LLM reseller xcai[.]pro (CrowdStrike), plus Storm-0940 infrastructure 144.172.64[.]60, .99, and .128 (Microsoft). Treat them as perishable: Censys watched 10 attacker open directories close and 15 new ones appear in two days. For ARTEX mitigation, rate-limit by account, session, and API key rather than IP alone, enforce API authorization server-side, and issue short-lived credentials. Decoys and tarpits work unusually well here, because an autonomous agent will happily burn its token budget on fake assets. Every Active Threats report linked above ships ready-to-deploy Sigma and AI rules plus simulation scripts, so you can validate coverage before ARTEX tests it for you. PHP2shell ARTEX PHP2Shell is the bug class an agentic framework loves most: pre-auth, widespread, and with public PoCs. CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are RCE chains in PHP core’s session.upload_progress, rated CVSS v4 9.2 and affecting PHP 5.4.0 through 8.5.11. PHP shipped fixes on October 21, 2026, a day early after the CVE IDs leaked ( Arctic Wolf ). The ARTEX PoC angle is concrete. An issue on an ARTEX fork proposed a php2shell-check skill that vendors three public verification scripts from the php2shell-poc research repo. Once a check like that exists as a skill, the Planner can queue it as just another intent against every PHP asset in the graph. The exposure is huge. Qualys counted 167 million PHP installations, 71% of them on end-of-life versions that will never get a vendor patch ( Qualys ). Amazon caught an exploitation attempt in its MadPot honeypots on October 17, four days before disclosure. To hunt PHP2Shell in ARTEX-style traffic, look for: Multipart POSTs carrying a PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field with attacker-chosen session IDs Follow-up file inclusion requests pointing at sess_ files in PHP session directories Inert PHP canaries and unique output markers, which scanners use to confirm evaluation PHP worker processes spawning shells, curl, or wget Patch first, upgrade end-of-life branches, and disable upload progress tracking where applications do not need it. FAQ What is ARTEX and how does it work? An open-source, LLM-driven pentest framework. Planner and Worker agents loop through recon, probing, and exploitation toward an operator-defined goal. When was ARTEX first discovered? It was released July 26, 2026. CrowdStrike first reported malicious use on October 7, 2026. What is the impact of ARTEX on systems? Data theft, RAT deployment, cloud identity takeover, and supply-chain compromise across finance, IT, and software vendors. Can ARTEX still affect me in 2026? Yes. Forks and rebrands remain active, and Censys still tracks 1,400+ exposed consoles. How can I protect myself from ARTEX? Patch fast (PHP2Shell first), rate-limit by identity, harden IdP flows, and deploy decoys. How can I detect ARTEX? Correlate volumetric web, identity, and cloud anomalies. Full details for ARTEX rules live in the SOC Prime reports linked above.

items.title: EU Accuses Temu of Failing to Stop Illegal Products, Citing Weak Security and Moderation Controls
items.summary: The European Commission has preliminarily found Temu in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA), citing weak product checks, poor content moderation, and ineffective penalties against sellers. Announced on November 17, 2026, the findings question whether the marketplace takes effective steps to stop illegal products from reaching European buyers. The case concerns Article 35, which requires platforms to put concrete measures in place to reduce identified risks. These are preliminary findings, not a final ruling. Although the concerns involve platform security controls, the announcement does not describe a data breach, malware attack, or confirmed compromise of Temu’s systems. Investigators found that Temu requests product test reports for only a very small share of listings. Even when sellers must submit these reports, the company often does not check them. This leaves a gap between collecting safety documents and confirming that goods actually meet European Union safety requirements. Temu Breaching Digital Services Act Temu classifies toys, electronics, and cosmetics as high risk, but allegedly does not give them priority during physical inspections. The Commission also found that the company often failed to follow up on spot check results. Inspection levels did not increase as the number of product listings grew. The findings show why risk controls must grow alongside online services. Related Cybersecurity News coverage of EU platform oversight explains how DSA supervision extends to major digital services. For Temu, the immediate question is whether its checks can identify unsafe goods, rather than simply process an expanding volume of listings. According to the Commission, Temu’s moderation focuses mainly on listing information and compliance with its own terms, rather than product safety. Its system for comparing listings with previously flagged goods also gives insufficient attention to unsafe products. Separately, an approved corrective action plan requires Temu to examine moderation limits and possible seller manipulation. Human review presents another weakness. The number of moderators has not kept pace with listing growth, the Commission said. Taken together, these findings describe gaps across document checks, listing comparisons, physical inspections, and staff review. A listing that meets website rules does not necessarily prove the product itself is safe. The Commission also questioned penalties aimed at individual stores instead of the traders behind them. One trader can operate several stores, allowing sales to continue elsewhere after a closure. Investigators found that sellers could commit numerous serious violations, including failed product safety checks, before Temu suspended any of their stores. Temu can inspect the investigation file and respond in writing. The European Board for Digital Services will also be consulted. If confirmed, the findings could bring corrective orders and a fine reaching 6% of worldwide annual turnover. This differs from the DMA framework covered in Cybersecurity News’ Google enforcement report . The new case follows a €200 million fine in May 2026 over inadequate risk assessment. Approval of Temu’s October action plan addressed that earlier breach, not the latest findings. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

Separately, an approved corrective action plan requires Temu to examine moderation limits and possible seller manipulation.

Human review presents another weakness. The number of moderators has not kept pace with listing growth, the Commission said. Taken together, these findings describe gaps across document checks, listing comparisons, physical inspections, and staff review. A listing that meets website rules does not necessarily prove the product itself is safe.

The Commission also questioned penalties aimed at individual stores instead of the traders behind them. One trader can operate several stores, allowing sales to continue elsewhere after a closure. Investigators found that sellers could commit numerous serious violations, including failed product safety checks, before Temu suspended any of their stores.

Temu can inspect the investigation file and respond in writing. The European Board for Digital Services will also be consulted. If confirmed, the findings could bring corrective orders and a fine reaching 6% of worldwide annual turnover. This differs from the DMA framework covered in Cybersecurity News’ Google enforcement report.

The new case follows a €200 million fine in May 2026 over inadequate risk assessment. Approval of Temu’s October action plan addressed that earlier breach, not the latest findings.

items.summary_html:
On Monday, the Council of the EU sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities for Russian information manipulation and malicious cyber activity. The influence side hits the Social Design Agency, the Moscow political-technology firm behind years of fake-news operations. The cyber side lists NoName057(16), the pro-Russian group that has spent four years knocking European websites offline with DDoS attacks. 

A sanctions listing won't take down a botnet, and nobody in Brussels expects it to. What it changes is the legal exposure for every European company that might pay, host, employ or do business with anyone on the list.  

It also puts a propaganda shop and a DDoS crew in the same announcement, which tells defenders how the EU now sees them - two arms of one hybrid campaign. 

What the Council announced 

The Council's announcement covers two separate legal regimes: 

  • Russia's destabilizing activities regime, created Oct. 8, 2024, adds the Social Design Agency, 24 of its staff and six pro-Kremlin commentators. It now lists 111 individuals and 21 entities. The EU's diplomatic service calls this the largest EU sanctions package targeting foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI) to date. 

  • The EU's horizontal cyber sanctions regime, in force since 2019, adds NoName057(16). It now lists 27 individuals and 12 entities. 

The effects are the standard ones. Assets in the EU are frozen, EU citizens and companies may not make funds available to anyone listed, directly or indirectly, and listed individuals can't enter or transit the EU. The listings came on the same day as a separate package of 113 names aimed at Russia's war financing. 

Who's on the list 

The Social Design Agency runs the Doppelgänger campaign, which clones real news sites to spread fake stories. It has been under EU sanctions over the war in Ukraine since 2023. This listing moves it under the regime aimed at operations against the EU itself. The Council alleges that the agency's major operations need sign-off from Sergey Kiriyenko, first deputy chief of staff in Russia's presidential administration, and accuses it of cloning news sites, building Wikipedia-style platforms and staging physical provocations around the 2024 European Parliament elections. 

The 24 staff listed go well beyond management. Alongside Andrey Perla, named as the agency's "chief ideologue," the list includes caricaturists, monitors, a system administrator and the editor of "Pulse," an internal network of Telegram channels. Britain had already sanctioned 22 of them. 

The six commentators include RT correspondent Chay Bowes, accused of amplifying the Storm-1516 operation, and military blogger Yurii Podoliaka, who the EU says raised more than 1 billion rubles for Russian forces. 

NoName057(16) emerged in March 2022. The Council says it hit energy, finance, transport, and water sites with DDoS attacks, along with political parties and candidates during elections. Europol's Operation Eastwood took more than 100 of its servers offline in July 2025, and the group kept going. 

The target is the supply chain, not the operators 

The skeptical read is easy. A caricaturist in Moscow probably holds nothing in the EU worth freezing, and a DDoS crew that survived a 12-country police operation won't fold over an asset freeze. 

But influence and DDoS operations run on Western infrastructure. Domains, hosting, ad networks, payment rails, crypto exchanges and freelancers. Doppelgänger needed lookalike domains on Western registrars, which is why the U.S. Justice Department seized a batch of them in 2024. NoName057(16) paid its volunteers in cryptocurrency, Europol said. The "directly or indirectly" clause pushes the enforcement burden onto every EU company in those chains. 

The regime choice matters too. The destabilization regime gives Brussels extra tools for later, including bans on transactions involving physical infrastructure such as servers and network equipment. That is a lever aimed squarely at hosting providers. 

The pairing is the other signal. The Council's own descriptions put SDA provocations around elections next to NoName057(16) DDoS attacks on parties and candidates during elections. When a party's website goes down on election week, the outage is the smaller part of the attack. The headline it creates is the point. 

Who's affected 

Two groups of European organizations should read the list closely. 

The first is anyone who could end up providing money or services to a listed party, which includes banks, payment processors, crypto exchanges, hosting and cloud providers, domain registrars, ad networks, and PR or media firms that hire freelance writers and designers. Sanctions screening also has to cover entities owned or controlled by a listed person, even if they aren't named. 

The second is NoName057(16)'s target list, which includes government portals, energy, finance, transport and water operators, and political parties. For them, the sanctions change nothing operationally. The DDoS traffic will keep coming. 

Plan of action 

  1. Refresh screening today. Pull the new names from the Official Journal acts (Council Implementing Regulations 2026/2558 and 2026/2550) into your sanctions screening, and rescreen vendors, freelancers and customers, not just payment counterparties. 

  1. Hosting providers and registrars: tighten customer checks. Doppelgängers depend on lookalike domains and cheap hosting. Make sure abuse reports about cloned news sites reach someone who can act on them quickly. 

  1. Watch for clones of your own brand. If you run a news outlet, a public body or a well-known consumer brand, monitor for lookalike domains and copied pages. Doppelgängers' method is to wear a trusted name. 

  1. Plan for election-week DDoS. If you're a party, a public body or critical infrastructure, test DDoS protection on public sites before the next vote. NoName057(16) announces its targets on Telegram, so put its channels in your threat feeds. 

  1. Prepare the message as well as the mitigation. A short holding statement that explains the outage and says whether any data was affected takes away most of the headline an attacker wanted. 

What we're watching 

NoName057(16) is changing tactics. U.S. prosecutors charged an alleged member in September, and researchers recently tied the group to a campaign that published personal details of senior European officials on the dark web, with crypto rewards offered for more. Doxxing aimed at officials and their families is a harder problem than a website outage. 

Spotting that exposure early matters. Cyble monitors dark web forums, leak sites, and Telegram channels for leaked credentials and personal data tied to your executives and staff, so your team can respond before the information is used against them. Request a demo to see how it works. 

The other question is whether Brussels uses the infrastructure-transaction bans the destabilization regime allows. If it does, hosting and network providers will feel these listings far more than the people named in them. 

Key takeaways 

  • On Nov. 16, 2026, the EU sanctioned 30 individuals and two entities: the Social Design Agency with 24 staff and six commentators under its Russia destabilization regime, and NoName057(16) under its cyber regime. 

  • The operators will barely feel it. The burden falls on EU banks, hosting providers, registrars, ad networks, and crypto platforms, which may not deal with anyone listed, directly or indirectly. 

  • Listing a propaganda firm and a DDoS crew together reflects one playbook: election-period disruption built for headlines. 

  • Update screening lists now, monitor for clones of your brand, and plan DDoS defense and messaging before the next election. 

Sources 

  • Council of the EU, Russia's FIMI and malicious cyber activities: Council imposes sanctions on 30 individuals and two entities, Nov. 16, 2026 

  • Council Decision (CFSP) 2026/2556, Nov. 16, 2026 

  • EEAS, The EU extends sanctions to nearly all major Russian banks, Nov. 16, 2026 

  • Brussels Times, EU sanctions target Moscow-linked propaganda agency, hacker group, Nov. 16, 2026

items.title: Microsoft Windows 11 Secretly Tracks Which AI Coding Agents Developers Use Through Telemetry
items.summary: Windows 11 has a built-in component that notes which AI coding agents and developer tools you run. It sends that data to Microsoft if optional diagnostic data is on. Security researcher Xusheng Li, who works on Binary Ninja, shared the first finding on X on November 16, 2026. He then published a full technical write-up . Windows 11 AI Agent Tracking Li asked an AI helper to look through recent Windows files for undocumented features. It flagged a list of names inside MissionControlAggregator.dll, including codex.exe, claude.exe, copilot.exe, and cursor.exe. The same list held common tools like python.exe, dotnet.exe, gcc.exe, and code.exe. Li opened the file in Binary Ninja and found that the names were used in simple comparisons. A feature flag called CLICodingAgentUsage guards the new checks. Binary Ninja Agent Strings (Image Source: Xusheng) The DLL does not scan your running programs. It listens to events Windows already creates, such as KernelProcess.AppStateChangeSummary and Win32kTraceLogging.AppInteractivitySummary. It also reads WSL launch events. A normal Windows copy of codex.exe can trigger a match, so the check is not limited to Linux tools. When a name matches, the component sets a bit in its saved state. Later, it sends a report called Segments.SubCohorts through Event Tracing for Windows . The report holds only yes-or-no flags, not runtime, focus time, or prompt text. Even so, a list of the AI tools a developer uses is private information. Li checked a Windows 11 ARM64 virtual machine on build 26200.9974. The feature was already on, and the DiagTrack telemetry service was running. DiagTrack started AggregatorHost.exe, which loaded the DLL. To test it, he copied cmd.exe and renamed it codex.exe. The name alone was enough to set the Codex bit. A report then showed CliAgentSubCohorts with a value of 4. A copy renamed gcc.exe set a separate developer-tool bit. Li did not stop at the local event, because local logs alone prove nothing. He found that a DiagTrack listener was subscribed to the report. The report also appeared in DiagTrack’s upload queue, marked as not required. That means Microsoft treats it as optional diagnostic data. On a clean US install of Windows 11 Home, optional data was on by default, and AllowTelemetry was set to 3. A baseline VM from the public ISO had the coding-agent feature off. So this is not proven to be active on every Windows PC. Windows Optional Diagnostic Settings (Image Source: Xusheng) Open Settings, then Privacy & security, then Diagnostics & feedback. Turn off Send optional diagnostic data. Microsoft’s own diagnostics and privacy guide says your device stays secure and works normally with only required data. It also says optional data can include device activity, which fits this case. Managed work PCs may hide this setting, so IT teams should check their own policies. AI coding tools already draw attention from bad actors. Cyber Security News recently reported that info-stealing malware now targets Claude, Cursor, and Codex data saved on developer machines. It also covered new threats against AI coding tools that steal credentials. A record of who uses which agent is not a secret key, but it shows where valuable code and tokens may sit. Microsoft has not yet explained why it collects this data. It may be for product planning, since Windows is adding more agent features. Until the company speaks, developers should check their diagnostic settings, read Li’s evidence, and decide what they are comfortable sharing. items.title: CVE-2026-99288: NoisyTCP Linux Kernel Flaw Enables Remote Server Crashes
items.summary: A newly disclosed Linux kernel vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP , can enable an unauthenticated remote attacker to crash vulnerable Linux systems by sending specially crafted TCP traffic to an exposed listening service. The issue resides in the kernel TCP networking subsystem and can affect common server workloads such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH without requiring authentication or an unusual application configuration. The vulnerability remained in the Linux kernel for roughly 11 years after being introduced in October 2015. Red Hat rates the issue Important with a CVSS 3.1 score of 7.5 , noting that successful exploitation can cause an operating-system-level denial of service. Current public research does not demonstrate arbitrary code execution as a reliable attack outcome. The risk is particularly relevant to organizations operating internet-facing Linux infrastructure because exploitation occurs before authentication. If a vulnerable service running inside a container is targeted, the resulting kernel panic can affect the underlying host rather than only the individual container, potentially disrupting multiple workloads simultaneously. Organizations can strengthen their defenses against emerging vulnerability exploitation with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, helping security teams operationalize threat intelligence and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Detect CVE-2026-99288 by monitoring suspicious TCP behavior preceding kernel instability, unexpected host reboots, and Linux kernel panic events on externally reachable systems. Since NoisyTCP operates at the kernel networking layer, defenders should correlate host-level telemetry with network activity instead of relying exclusively on application logs. Contact Sales CVE-2026-99288 analysis CVE-2026-99288 affects the Linux kernel’s TCP established-socket lookup logic. TCP established ehash lookups operate without traditional locking, while the relevant socket caches use SLAB_TYPESAFE_BY_RCU, which allows memory to be reused before an RCU reader holding the previous address has completed its operation. After finding a matching tuple, functions such as __inet_lookup_established() and __inet6_lookup_established() obtain a reference and repeat the tuple validation. The vulnerable implementation does not verify whether the replacement object is already hashed. If memory is reused for another socket with the same tuple, a stale lookup can therefore acquire a reference to the new object before it is fully integrated into the expected socket state. One demonstrated attack path involves the reuse of a request socket through SYN cookies. While one receive context retains a stale reference to an existing request socket, another context can free that object and allocate a new SYN cookie request at the same slab address. Because the tuple remains the same, the stale lookup can acquire a reference to the replacement object and pass the tuple check. The newly created request socket, however, has not yet been hashed and has a NULL rsk_listener. When the Linux TCP receive path later attempts to use the listener, it dereferences the NULL pointer. This results in a kernel panic and causes the operating system to crash. Successful exploitation requires the stale lookup and socket reuse to occur concurrently in separate receive contexts. Researchers found that this can be achieved by exploiting differences in receive hashing between IPv4 fragments and ordinary TCP packets. Consequently, systems with two or more RX queues, or environments where Receive Packet Steering distributes traffic across multiple CPUs, can provide the concurrency necessary to trigger the race. The CVE-2026-99288 PoC demonstrates that exploitation time depends heavily on the target environment. Against Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running with default configurations on QEMU/KVM virtual machines, the researcher was able to reproduce the crash in approximately five seconds to two minutes. By comparison, triggering the issue on a quiet bare-metal Nginx server with eight RX queues took roughly 14 hours even with race timing tuned for the specific system. Virtualization can make the race more practical because vCPU preemption introduces additional scheduling variance. Nevertheless, the underlying weakness is not limited to virtual machines or a specific server application. Any directly reachable vulnerable Linux host exposing a TCP listener can potentially be targeted when the required concurrency conditions exist. The vulnerability originated in Linux kernel commit 079096f103fa, introduced on October 3, 2015 with Linux 4.4. The upstream correction, commit 4e2b3ef19e0e, was merged on November 3, 2026. The fix causes established socket lookups to reject unhashed objects, release the acquired reference, and restart the lookup instead of continuing with an unsafe reused socket. The Linux kernel CVE team lists 6.12.117, 6.18.63, and 7.3.4 among the stable kernel versions containing the correction. However, distribution vendors can backport patches independently, so administrators should rely on the advisory for their specific Linux distribution rather than assume that a version number alone determines exposure. For CVE-2026-99288 detection, security teams should correlate Linux kernel logs, system availability telemetry, and network activity. Potential indicators include kernel NULL pointer dereference events, kernel panics associated with tcp_v4_rcv, unexplained server reboots, and unusual bursts of TCP traffic immediately preceding system failure. Traditional CVE-2026-99288 IOCs such as malicious file hashes, payload URLs, or attacker-controlled domains are less relevant because exploitation can occur entirely through network traffic without dropping malware on the target. Defenders should therefore prioritize behavioral evidence, crash telemetry, TCP connection patterns, fragmentation activity, SYN traffic, and repeated host resets. As of November 17, 2026, there is no confirmed evidence that the vulnerability is being actively exploited in real-world attacks. Public research demonstrates remote denial of service, while Red Hat explicitly states that exploitation does not provide data modification or arbitrary code execution. Security teams seeking additional details for CVE-2026-99288 should consult the Linux kernel CVE announcement, vendor-specific advisories, and the original NoisyTCP disclosure because fixed package versions and backport availability can vary significantly across Linux distributions. CVE-2026-99288 Mitigation The most effective remediation is to install an updated kernel containing the upstream correction or the corresponding security backport supplied by the Linux distribution vendor. The Linux kernel CVE team recommends updating to the latest stable kernel rather than cherry-picking an individual change whenever possible. For CVE-2026-99288 mitigation, organizations should first inventory externally reachable Linux servers and identify systems exposing TCP services such as Nginx, Apache, SSH, proxies, gateways, and other network-facing workloads. Virtual machines with multiple RX queues, environments using RPS, and hosts supporting multiple critical containers should receive particularly high patching priority. Administrators should verify their running kernel rather than only checking whether the operating system’s package manager recently installed updates. A patched kernel package does not protect the system until the server has rebooted into that kernel. When immediate patching is not possible, Hyunwoo Kim and Red Hat document two temporary mitigations. One approach is to disable SYN cookies: sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0 This prevents the demonstrated path in which a request socket is reconstructed through a SYN cookie. However, disabling the feature reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, so administrators should carefully evaluate the operational and security trade-offs. The setting is maintained per network namespace and may therefore need to be applied individually to containers using separate namespaces. A second temporary measure is to reduce packet handling to a single RX queue and disable Receive Packet Steering and Receive Flow Steering. Since exploitation depends on separate RX contexts racing concurrently, serializing packet processing can prevent the demonstrated condition. This approach can affect network performance and should be evaluated before deployment in production environments. Organizations should additionally reduce unnecessary public exposure of administrative and infrastructure services, restrict TCP access to trusted networks where operationally possible, and ensure centralized collection of kernel logs and crash telemetry. These controls cannot substitute for patching but can help reduce attack surface and improve incident investigation. FAQ What is CVE-2026-99288 and how does it work? CVE-2026-99288, also known as NoisyTCP, is a Linux kernel TCP race condition affecting lockless established-socket lookups. Under specific timing conditions, recycled socket memory can be referenced before the replacement object has been fully initialized and hashed. A remote attacker can manipulate TCP traffic to trigger a NULL pointer dereference, resulting in a kernel panic and denial of service. When was CVE-2026-99288 first discovered? The precise date on which Hyunwoo Kim privately discovered the vulnerability has not been publicly disclosed. The correction entered the Linux networking development process in late October 2026 and was merged upstream on November 3. The Linux kernel CNA publicly announced the vulnerability on November 10, 2026, while Kim released the detailed NoisyTCP research after the coordinated disclosure embargo expired on November 15–16. What is the impact of CVE-2026-99288 on systems? Successful exploitation can remotely crash the Linux kernel and take the entire operating system offline without authentication. If the affected host runs containers or multiple services, a kernel panic can disrupt all workloads sharing that kernel. Current evidence demonstrates denial of service rather than reliable remote code execution. Can CVE-2026-99288 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Systems remain exposed when they run a vulnerable kernel that does not contain the upstream correction or a vendor backport. Because the underlying bug dates back to Linux 4.4 in 2015, many kernel branches and Linux distributions may be affected. Administrators should verify the latest security advisory for their distribution because patch availability continues to change as vendors release backports. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-99288? Apply a vendor-provided kernel update containing the NoisyTCP correction and reboot the system into the patched kernel. If immediate updating is impossible, evaluate temporary measures such as disabling SYN cookies or reducing packet processing to a single RX queue with RPS and RFS disabled. Organizations should also limit unnecessary TCP exposure and monitor Linux hosts for kernel panics, unexpected reboots, and suspicious network activity.

A newly disclosed Linux kernel vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-99288 and dubbed NoisyTCP, can enable an unauthenticated remote attacker to crash vulnerable Linux systems by sending specially crafted TCP traffic to an exposed listening service. The issue resides in the kernel TCP networking subsystem and can affect common server workloads such as Nginx, Apache, and SSH without requiring authentication or an unusual application configuration.

The vulnerability remained in the Linux kernel for roughly 11 years after being introduced in October 2015. Red Hat rates the issue Important with a CVSS 3.1 score of 7.5, noting that successful exploitation can cause an operating-system-level denial of service. Current public research does not demonstrate arbitrary code execution as a reliable attack outcome.

The risk is particularly relevant to organizations operating internet-facing Linux infrastructure because exploitation occurs before authentication. If a vulnerable service running inside a container is targeted, the resulting kernel panic can affect the underlying host rather than only the individual container, potentially disrupting multiple workloads simultaneously.

Organizations can strengthen their defenses against emerging vulnerability exploitation with SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform, helping security teams operationalize threat intelligence and accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Detect CVE-2026-99288 by monitoring suspicious TCP behavior preceding kernel instability, unexpected host reboots, and Linux kernel panic events on externally reachable systems. Since NoisyTCP operates at the kernel networking layer, defenders should correlate host-level telemetry with network activity instead of relying exclusively on application logs.

Contact Sales

CVE-2026-99288 analysis

CVE-2026-99288 affects the Linux kernel’s TCP established-socket lookup logic. TCP established ehash lookups operate without traditional locking, while the relevant socket caches use SLAB_TYPESAFE_BY_RCU, which allows memory to be reused before an RCU reader holding the previous address has completed its operation.

After finding a matching tuple, functions such as __inet_lookup_established() and __inet6_lookup_established() obtain a reference and repeat the tuple validation. The vulnerable implementation does not verify whether the replacement object is already hashed. If memory is reused for another socket with the same tuple, a stale lookup can therefore acquire a reference to the new object before it is fully integrated into the expected socket state.

One demonstrated attack path involves the reuse of a request socket through SYN cookies. While one receive context retains a stale reference to an existing request socket, another context can free that object and allocate a new SYN cookie request at the same slab address. Because the tuple remains the same, the stale lookup can acquire a reference to the replacement object and pass the tuple check.

The newly created request socket, however, has not yet been hashed and has a NULL rsk_listener. When the Linux TCP receive path later attempts to use the listener, it dereferences the NULL pointer. This results in a kernel panic and causes the operating system to crash.

Successful exploitation requires the stale lookup and socket reuse to occur concurrently in separate receive contexts. Researchers found that this can be achieved by exploiting differences in receive hashing between IPv4 fragments and ordinary TCP packets. Consequently, systems with two or more RX queues, or environments where Receive Packet Steering distributes traffic across multiple CPUs, can provide the concurrency necessary to trigger the race.

The CVE-2026-99288 PoC demonstrates that exploitation time depends heavily on the target environment. Against Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers running with default configurations on QEMU/KVM virtual machines, the researcher was able to reproduce the crash in approximately five seconds to two minutes. By comparison, triggering the issue on a quiet bare-metal Nginx server with eight RX queues took roughly 14 hours even with race timing tuned for the specific system.

Virtualization can make the race more practical because vCPU preemption introduces additional scheduling variance. Nevertheless, the underlying weakness is not limited to virtual machines or a specific server application. Any directly reachable vulnerable Linux host exposing a TCP listener can potentially be targeted when the required concurrency conditions exist.

The vulnerability originated in Linux kernel commit 079096f103fa, introduced on October 3, 2015 with Linux 4.4. The upstream correction, commit 4e2b3ef19e0e, was merged on November 3, 2026. The fix causes established socket lookups to reject unhashed objects, release the acquired reference, and restart the lookup instead of continuing with an unsafe reused socket.

The Linux kernel CVE team lists 6.12.117, 6.18.63, and 7.3.4 among the stable kernel versions containing the correction. However, distribution vendors can backport patches independently, so administrators should rely on the advisory for their specific Linux distribution rather than assume that a version number alone determines exposure.

For CVE-2026-99288 detection, security teams should correlate Linux kernel logs, system availability telemetry, and network activity. Potential indicators include kernel NULL pointer dereference events, kernel panics associated with tcp_v4_rcv, unexplained server reboots, and unusual bursts of TCP traffic immediately preceding system failure.

Traditional CVE-2026-99288 IOCs such as malicious file hashes, payload URLs, or attacker-controlled domains are less relevant because exploitation can occur entirely through network traffic without dropping malware on the target. Defenders should therefore prioritize behavioral evidence, crash telemetry, TCP connection patterns, fragmentation activity, SYN traffic, and repeated host resets.

As of November 17, 2026, there is no confirmed evidence that the vulnerability is being actively exploited in real-world attacks. Public research demonstrates remote denial of service, while Red Hat explicitly states that exploitation does not provide data modification or arbitrary code execution.

Security teams seeking additional details for CVE-2026-99288 should consult the Linux kernel CVE announcement, vendor-specific advisories, and the original NoisyTCP disclosure because fixed package versions and backport availability can vary significantly across Linux distributions.

CVE-2026-99288 Mitigation

The most effective remediation is to install an updated kernel containing the upstream correction or the corresponding security backport supplied by the Linux distribution vendor. The Linux kernel CVE team recommends updating to the latest stable kernel rather than cherry-picking an individual change whenever possible.

For CVE-2026-99288 mitigation, organizations should first inventory externally reachable Linux servers and identify systems exposing TCP services such as Nginx, Apache, SSH, proxies, gateways, and other network-facing workloads. Virtual machines with multiple RX queues, environments using RPS, and hosts supporting multiple critical containers should receive particularly high patching priority.

Administrators should verify their running kernel rather than only checking whether the operating system’s package manager recently installed updates. A patched kernel package does not protect the system until the server has rebooted into that kernel.

When immediate patching is not possible, Hyunwoo Kim and Red Hat document two temporary mitigations. One approach is to disable SYN cookies:

sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0

This prevents the demonstrated path in which a request socket is reconstructed through a SYN cookie. However, disabling the feature reduces protection against SYN flood attacks, so administrators should carefully evaluate the operational and security trade-offs. The setting is maintained per network namespace and may therefore need to be applied individually to containers using separate namespaces.

A second temporary measure is to reduce packet handling to a single RX queue and disable Receive Packet Steering and Receive Flow Steering. Since exploitation depends on separate RX contexts racing concurrently, serializing packet processing can prevent the demonstrated condition. This approach can affect network performance and should be evaluated before deployment in production environments.

Organizations should additionally reduce unnecessary public exposure of administrative and infrastructure services, restrict TCP access to trusted networks where operationally possible, and ensure centralized collection of kernel logs and crash telemetry. These controls cannot substitute for patching but can help reduce attack surface and improve incident investigation.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-99288 and how does it work?

CVE-2026-99288, also known as NoisyTCP, is a Linux kernel TCP race condition affecting lockless established-socket lookups. Under specific timing conditions, recycled socket memory can be referenced before the replacement object has been fully initialized and hashed. A remote attacker can manipulate TCP traffic to trigger a NULL pointer dereference, resulting in a kernel panic and denial of service.

When was CVE-2026-99288 first discovered?

The precise date on which Hyunwoo Kim privately discovered the vulnerability has not been publicly disclosed. The correction entered the Linux networking development process in late October 2026 and was merged upstream on November 3. The Linux kernel CNA publicly announced the vulnerability on November 10, 2026, while Kim released the detailed NoisyTCP research after the coordinated disclosure embargo expired on November 15–16.

What is the impact of CVE-2026-99288 on systems?

Successful exploitation can remotely crash the Linux kernel and take the entire operating system offline without authentication. If the affected host runs containers or multiple services, a kernel panic can disrupt all workloads sharing that kernel. Current evidence demonstrates denial of service rather than reliable remote code execution.

Can CVE-2026-99288 still affect me in 2026?

Yes. Systems remain exposed when they run a vulnerable kernel that does not contain the upstream correction or a vendor backport. Because the underlying bug dates back to Linux 4.4 in 2015, many kernel branches and Linux distributions may be affected. Administrators should verify the latest security advisory for their distribution because patch availability continues to change as vendors release backports.

How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-99288?

Apply a vendor-provided kernel update containing the NoisyTCP correction and reboot the system into the patched kernel. If immediate updating is impossible, evaluate temporary measures such as disabling SYN cookies or reducing packet processing to a single RX queue with RPS and RFS disabled. Organizations should also limit unnecessary TCP exposure and monitor Linux hosts for kernel panics, unexpected reboots, and suspicious network activity.

items.summary: TL;DR: GhostMap is Aqua Nautilus’s research name for the Linux eBPF rootkit shared across examined IronWorm and Atomic Arch malware payloads. It blinds user-space applications by manipulating kernel data on the fly to hide malicious processes, files, and network sockets. In controlled experiments, Aqua Nautilus traced these evasion mechanics and proved their limits: while overwriting &mldr

items.title: “Amazon” job offer promises $5,000 a month, but it’s got all the signs of a scam
items.summary: Last month, Amazon announced plans to hire more than 300,000 people in the US for the holidays. That’s welcome news for job seekers, but scammers know that. We found several sites advertising a remote assistant job under Amazon-like names, with promises of up to $5,000 a month. None of the sites is run by Amazon. Amazon says all genuine job opportunities are posted on amazon.jobs ; hourly warehouse jobs are also listed at hiring.amazon.com . The offers we found are separate from Amazon’s holiday hiring push. The application doesn’t match the job description One careers page calls the role a “legitimate, fully remote position,” with “no commute, no office, no fixed desk.” Yet the form asks whether applicants have reliable access to a personal vehicle and someone at home who can receive packages. Those questions point to package handling, not remote assistant work. A recruitment page promises fully remote work paying up to $5,000 a month Why Amazon makes such good bait People expect Amazon to be hiring. A hiring announcement can make an “Amazon is hiring” message seem plausible. But the remote assistant jobs on these sites are separate from Amazon’s announced seasonal roles. “Working with Amazon” can sound believable. Businesses can provide services to Amazon sellers without being part of Amazon. The sites use names that resemble those of logistics or seller-support businesses, which can make the connection harder to judge at a glance. The pitch targets people looking for flexible work. “Work from home” and a few hours a day can appeal to parents, students, and people looking for a second job. The tactic has been used before. Amazon says it saw more reports of scammers posing as recruiters in September and October 2025. In June, we warned about Amazon job texts offering $250 to $500 a day for 60 to 90 minutes of work. The sites we found add a careers site, a company website, and a polished application form to make the offer look more convincing. Several names, apparent links We found multiple recruitment and application sites using Amazon-like branding: amzssapplication[.]com and jobsamzss[.]com , two careers pages for the “Remote Assistant” job applyamazonsp[.]com , an application form for the same job, under the name “Amazon Seller Pro LLC” The sites use byte-identical site icons. Their domains were registered through the same registrar between July 23 and October 26. These similarities suggest a connection, although they do not establish who operates each site. The same remote assistant pitch appears on another domain The recruitment pages list “HR” email addresses on three additional domains: amzncrew[.]com, joinamzn[.]com, and workatamzn[.]com. These addresses do not establish an affiliation with Amazon. To verify a job with Amazon itself, check its official job boards at amazon.jobs or hiring.amazon.com . Independent businesses serving Amazon sellers hire separately, so verify their offers by contacting the business through contact details you find independently. The recruitment pages link to amzshippings[.]com, a website advertising preparation and shipping services for Amazon sellers. That’s a newly registered domain with hidden ownership details. A remote job that asks about your car and doorstep Although the careers pages on these sites describe the role as fully remote, the application asks: “Do you have reliable access to a personal vehicle?” If not, it asks applicants to explain how they would transport packages. “If you’re not home, is there a person to receive parcels?” A remote assistant wouldn’t normally need to receive or transport packages. These questions are warning signs of reshipping , also known as parcel-mule fraud . The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) says that a job asking you to receive shipments, repackage them, and send them elsewhere is a reshipping scam. The goods may have been bought with stolen payment details, and people recruited this way can be left handling packages connected to fraud. The form collects personal information The application form asks applicants for personal information The form collects your name, phone, email, home address including apartment number, felony history, education and employment history. It promises “Your data is secure” and sends submissions through Formspree, a third-party form service. We could not establish who receives the information. The page also tells search engines not to index it. No resume is needed. Instead, the careers page says: “ Our HR team calls you directly … Keep your phone on — we don’t schedule in advance. “ In the page code, that note sits below a leftover template comment: “ PASTE YOUR TEXT HERE. ” The recruitment page’s footer states: “Amazon Shipping Services is not affiliated with or endorsed by Amazon.com, Inc.” What could happen if you apply? Sharing your details could expose you to identity theft . If you take the job, you could also be asked to move packages or money tied to fraud. Identity theft: Your name, contact details, and home address can be useful to criminals . Be especially cautious if anyone later asks for your Social Security number, bank details, or ID. Being drawn into fraud: If you receive or forward packages bought with stolen payment details, your address may be linked to their movement. Losing money: A fake employer might later send a check and ask you to return some of the money or use it to buy supplies. The FTC warns that fake checks can bounce after the money has been sent on. How to stay safe Find Amazon jobs on amazon.jobs. Amazon says genuine job opportunities are listed on its official job board. Check the domain, not the logo. Anyone can copy Amazon’s colors and branding. Be wary of high pay for little work , especially when there’s no résumé or scheduled interview. Don’t receive or forward packages for an employer you haven’t verified. Don’t send ID photos, your Social Security number, or money before verifying the employer. If you already applied, don’t give an unscheduled caller your bank details, ID, or money. If you shared sensitive information, follow the steps at IdentityTheft.gov and consider placing a credit freeze. How Malwarebytes helps Malwarebytes Browser Guard blocks scam pages like these. And if you’re not sure whether a job offer is real, give the link or put a screenshot of the offer into Malwarebytes Scam Guard before you reply. It will assess whether it’s a scam and give you advice on what to do next. One careers page calls the role a “legitimate, fully remote position,” with “no commute, no office, no fixed desk.” Yet the form asks whether applicants have reliable access to a personal vehicle and someone at home who can receive packages. Those questions point to package handling, not remote assistant work.

A recruitment page promises fully remote work paying up to $5,000 a monthWhy Amazon makes such good bait

People expect Amazon to be hiring. A hiring announcement can make an “Amazon is hiring” message seem plausible. But the remote assistant jobs on these sites are separate from Amazon’s announced seasonal roles.

“Working with Amazon” can sound believable. Businesses can provide services to Amazon sellers without being part of Amazon. The sites use names that resemble those of logistics or seller-support businesses, which can make the connection harder to judge at a glance.

The pitch targets people looking for flexible work. “Work from home” and a few hours a day can appeal to parents, students, and people looking for a second job.

The tactic has been used before. Amazon says it saw more reports of scammers posing as recruiters in September and October 2025. In June, we warned about Amazon job texts offering $250 to $500 a day for 60 to 90 minutes of work. The sites we found add a careers site, a company website, and a polished application form to make the offer look more convincing.

Several names, apparent links

We found multiple recruitment and application sites using Amazon-like branding:

  • amzssapplication[.]com and jobsamzss[.]com, two careers pages for the “Remote Assistant” job
  • applyamazonsp[.]com, an application form for the same job, under the name “Amazon Seller Pro LLC”

The sites use byte-identical site icons. Their domains were registered through the same registrar between July 23 and October 26. These similarities suggest a connection, although they do not establish who operates each site.

The same remote assistant pitch appears on another domain

The recruitment pages list “HR” email addresses on three additional domains: amzncrew[.]com, joinamzn[.]com, and workatamzn[.]com. These addresses do not establish an affiliation with Amazon.

To verify a job with Amazon itself, check its official job boards at amazon.jobs or hiring.amazon.com. Independent businesses serving Amazon sellers hire separately, so verify their offers by contacting the business through contact details you find independently.

The recruitment pages link to amzshippings[.]com, a website advertising preparation and shipping services for Amazon sellers. That’s a newly registered domain with hidden ownership details.

A remote job that asks about your car and doorstep

Although the careers pages on these sites describe the role as fully remote, the application asks:

  • “Do you have reliable access to a personal vehicle?” If not, it asks applicants to explain how they would transport packages.
  • “If you’re not home, is there a person to receive parcels?”

A remote assistant wouldn’t normally need to receive or transport packages. These questions are warning signs of reshipping, also known as parcel-mule fraud.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) says that a job asking you to receive shipments, repackage them, and send them elsewhere is a reshipping scam. The goods may have been bought with stolen payment details, and people recruited this way can be left handling packages connected to fraud.

The form collects personal informationThe application form asks applicants for personal information

The form collects your name, phone, email, home address including apartment number, felony history, education and employment history. It promises “Your data is secure” and sends submissions through Formspree, a third-party form service. We could not establish who receives the information. The page also tells search engines not to index it.

No resume is needed. Instead, the careers page says: “Our HR team calls you directly … Keep your phone on — we don’t schedule in advance.“

In the page code, that note sits below a leftover template comment: “PASTE YOUR TEXT HERE.”

The recruitment page’s footer states: “Amazon Shipping Services is not affiliated with or endorsed by Amazon.com, Inc.”

What could happen if you apply?

Sharing your details could expose you to identity theft. If you take the job, you could also be asked to move packages or money tied to fraud.

  • Identity theft: Your name, contact details, and home address can be useful to criminals. Be especially cautious if anyone later asks for your Social Security number, bank details, or ID.
  • Being drawn into fraud: If you receive or forward packages bought with stolen payment details, your address may be linked to their movement.
  • Losing money: A fake employer might later send a check and ask you to return some of the money or use it to buy supplies. The FTC warns that fake checks can bounce after the money has been sent on.
How to stay safe
  • Find Amazon jobs on amazon.jobs. Amazon says genuine job opportunities are listed on its official job board.
  • Check the domain, not the logo. Anyone can copy Amazon’s colors and branding.
  • Be wary of high pay for little work, especially when there’s no résumé or scheduled interview.
  • Don’t receive or forward packages for an employer you haven’t verified.
  • Don’t send ID photos, your Social Security number, or money before verifying the employer.

If you already applied, don’t give an unscheduled caller your bank details, ID, or money. If you shared sensitive information, follow the steps at IdentityTheft.gov and consider placing a credit freeze.

items.title: FBI Warns Hackers Abuse Google Search to Spread Gootloader Malware and Launch Ransomware Attacks
items.summary: The FBI has warned that cybercriminals are using poisoned search results and compromised WordPress websites to spread Gootloader malware, giving ransomware operators an entry point into business networks. The attacks turn searches for legal documents, contracts, and business information into opportunities to trick users into downloading malicious JavaScript files. In a November 16, 2026, FLASH advisory, the bureau said it had identified more than 1,000 infected WordPress websites and 216 domains controlled by the Gootloader administrator as of October. The FBI linked this infrastructure to more than $28 million in ransomware payments, showing how document searches can lead to costly network compromises. Analysts behind the FBI warning published through IC3.gov’s Gootloader advisory identified the malware as an initial access framework rather than a ransomware encryptor. It establishes the foothold attackers need to deliver additional tools, steal credentials, move between systems, and prepare follow-on attacks against organizations across multiple sectors. FBI Warns Hackers Abuse Google Search The campaign relies on search engine optimization poisoning, which pushes attacker-controlled content alongside legitimate resources. Between 2020 and 2026, operators targeted search phrases with limited competition, including jurisdiction-specific contract clauses. Earlier reporting on Gootloader’s blackhat SEO techniques documented how fake forum discussions and hidden keywords helped malicious pages match users’ document searches. Legal professionals remain a major target. The FBI described searches aimed at practicing attorneys, in-house counsel, law firm partners, privacy teams, and legal technology decision-makers. Compromised WordPress websites serve different roles, acting as lure pages, redirectors, traffic filters, or relay infrastructure. Hidden keyword links and arranged backlinks increase their visibility in search results. A traffic distribution system checks details such as a visitor’s country, referring page, cookies, and IP address before deciding which content to display. This filtering means visitors can receive different content from the same compromised site. The operation’s recent evolution includes WordPress comment-path abuse, geographic filtering, and a stronger focus on U.S. legal professionals. Once a victim opens the downloaded JavaScript, the infection can progress beyond the browser. The FBI traced earlier versions through ZIP-delivered scripts and Windows Script Host execution, followed by PowerShell, scheduled tasks, and registry-resident payloads. Previous research into Gootloader’s fileless ransomware delivery explains how later-stage components can run from memory after being stored in the registry. The advisory also maps activity involving defense evasion, credential theft, and lateral movement, including process injection, AMSI impairment, remote services, and pass-the-hash authentication. These capabilities explain why a single script execution deserves urgent investigation: deleting the original download does not remove every payload or restore trust in the affected computer. Detection, Containment, and WordPress Protection Defenders should connect browser downloads with script execution, PowerShell activity, persistence changes, and unusual network connections. Earlier reporting on Gootloader’s lateral movement activity described attackers progressing from a poisoned search result toward domain infrastructure. The FBI recommends collecting process trees, scheduled tasks, browser history, DNS records, proxy logs, and endpoint memory where appropriate. If an archive was downloaded but not opened, users should avoid extracting or previewing it and submit it through their organization’s security process. If JavaScript executed, disconnect network access and follow incident-response procedures. Change exposed credentials from a clean device after investigators assess the damage, and reimage systems when persistence, credential theft, or additional malware is confirmed. Prevention includes restricting Windows Script Host where unnecessary, controlling scripts with WDAC or AppLocker, and blocking unauthorized execution from user-writable folders. WordPress owners should patch software, remove unused components, enforce strong administrator authentication, and monitor file integrity. Recent coverage of Gootloader infrastructure disruption efforts also underscores why website cleanup and credential resets remain necessary after takedowns. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Source-listed artifact Investigative relevance easinvoker.exe Copied executable associated with DLL sideloading C:\Windows with a trailing space Mock trusted directory used for masquerading AmsiScanBuffer Function targeted for defense impairment bashupload.com Alternate upload destination mentioned for exfiltration Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . items.title: Reducing Microsoft Sentinel Costs Without Compromising Detection – Part 3: The DNS Quest
items.summary: In our previous blog, Reducing Microsoft Sentinel Costs Without Compromising Detection – Part 2: The Firewall Quest , we described the application of Summary rules to Firewall events. In this part of our blog series, we focus on another expensive log source, DNS. We will explore DNS events and how Summary Rules can be leveraged in this high-volume log source to effectively reduce Sentinel costs while maintaining detection capabilities. The malware that has been deployed on the device, encodes information gathered from the host (credentials, files, or even just host or network information) into subdomain request. The device then sends DNS queries to a domain controlled by the attacker, enabling the attacker to collect and decode the information while also using the same channel to send commands to the compromised host. DNS Tunneling Testing

In order to test one of the DNS Tunneling attack variations, base32 encoding in FQDN, we will use the following small Powershell script to generate DNS events that emulate this attack pattern. $Domain = "total-legitimate-domain.domain"
$Iterations = 25

function New-Base32String {
    param([int]$Length = 45)   # 63 = DNS label max
    $base32Chars = "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ234567".ToCharArray()
    -join (1..$Length | ForEach-Object { $base32Chars | Get-Random })
}

for ($i = 1; $i -le $Iterations; $i++) {
    $subdomain = New-Base32String -Length 45
    $fqdn = "$subdomain.$Domain"

    Write-Host "[$i] Querying TXT record for $fqdn..."

    try {
        (Resolve-DnsName -Name $fqdn -Type TXT).Strings
    }
    catch {
        Write-Warning "Query failed for $fqdn : $_"
    }

    Start-Sleep -Seconds 0   # optional delay between queries
}
