items.title: Formal Verification of the Signal Protocol Using AI
items.summary: This seems like a good thing: Google Deepmind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees­a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. […] The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work. Alternate link . Details : First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human ­ just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Technical paper .

items.title: Facebook may have access to your entire photo gallery
items.summary: .kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{padding-top:20px;padding-right:20px;padding-bottom:10px;padding-left:20px;}.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{column-gap:var(--global-kb-gap-sm, 1rem);}.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;}.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col > .aligncenter{width:100%;}.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{background-color:rgba(255, 229, 229, 0.83);}.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col:before{opacity:0.3;}.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6{position:relative;}@media all and (max-width: 1024px){.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}}@media all and (max-width: 767px){.kadence-column490145_7a0b89-a6 > .kt-inside-inner-col{flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;}} In this article Facebook’s photo suggestions feature could access your entire gallery through a single permission Italy fined Meta €805 million and says the privacy violation remains ongoing for some users Check Facebook’s photo permissions to control what it can access If you’ve given Facebook access to your phone’s photos, the app may be able to read your entire gallery, including pictures you never intended to share. Check your photo permissions if you want to limit that access. Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta €805 million (about $887 million) for accessing Android users’ entire camera rolls without specific consent or adequate disclosure. The regulator says the violation remains ongoing for some users, despite changes Meta has made. The decision concerns Facebook’s “Get camera roll suggestions when you’re browsing Facebook” feature. Launched in 2023, the idea is to use your photos and videos to suggest potential social media posts. You might be surprised to hear that Facebook can access every photo or video in your gallery if you’ve granted full photo access. That includes pictures of your kids, restaurant receipts, and that Wi-Fi password label you photographed awkwardly on the router behind the TV. But you might have granted that access without realizing it also enabled photo suggestions. That’s the problem, said the regulator. Facebook’s app requested access to the camera roll through a single permission that applies across the entire app, covering multiple features with different requirements. The Garante said: “The permission is preceded by a non-specific notice (’enable other features’) which does not make it clear to the user that they are also authorising suggestions from the camera roll.” One permission, lots of features Asking permission for lots of things via one request violated Article 122 of the Italian Data Protection Code, according to the regulator. That code is Italy’s privacy law, and its Article 122 implements the EU’s ePrivacy Directive, which protects data stored on devices such as smartphones. The Garante said access for this feature required free and informed consent. Facebook also failed to adequately explain its use of the photo gallery, and the suggestions feature was on by default. Granting full photo access could give the app ongoing access to the entire library, the regulator said, without users being able to verify which information was actually being used. The regulator’s investigation started in July 2025 after consumer organization Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti submitted a report. That prompted the Garante to conduct its own technical analysis. Meta had asked for Ireland to handle the case. Like many other technology companies, Meta’s main EU presence is in Ireland, whose regulator handles many cross-border privacy cases. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules at issue do not use that system. In this article
  • Facebook’s photo suggestions feature could access your entire gallery through a single permission
  • Italy fined Meta €805 million and says the privacy violation remains ongoing for some users
  • Check Facebook’s photo permissions to control what it can access

If you’ve given Facebook access to your phone’s photos, the app may be able to read your entire gallery, including pictures you never intended to share. Check your photo permissions if you want to limit that access.

Italy’s data protection authority, the Garante, has fined Meta €805 million (about $887 million) for accessing Android users’ entire camera rolls without specific consent or adequate disclosure. The regulator says the violation remains ongoing for some users, despite changes Meta has made.

The decision concerns Facebook’s “Get camera roll suggestions when you’re browsing Facebook” feature. Launched in 2023, the idea is to use your photos and videos to suggest potential social media posts.

You might be surprised to hear that Facebook can access every photo or video in your gallery if you’ve granted full photo access. That includes pictures of your kids, restaurant receipts, and that Wi-Fi password label you photographed awkwardly on the router behind the TV. But you might have granted that access without realizing it also enabled photo suggestions. That’s the problem, said the regulator.

Facebook’s app requested access to the camera roll through a single permission that applies across the entire app, covering multiple features with different requirements. The Garante said:

“The permission is preceded by a non-specific notice (’enable other features’) which does not make it clear to the user that they are also authorising suggestions from the camera roll.”

One permission, lots of features

Asking permission for lots of things via one request violated Article 122 of the Italian Data Protection Code, according to the regulator. That code is Italy’s privacy law, and its Article 122 implements the EU’s ePrivacy Directive, which protects data stored on devices such as smartphones. The Garante said access for this feature required free and informed consent.

Facebook also failed to adequately explain its use of the photo gallery, and the suggestions feature was on by default. Granting full photo access could give the app ongoing access to the entire library, the regulator said, without users being able to verify which information was actually being used.

The regulator’s investigation started in July 2025 after consumer organization Centro Tutela Consumatori Utenti submitted a report. That prompted the Garante to conduct its own technical analysis.

Meta had asked for Ireland to handle the case. Like many other technology companies, Meta’s main EU presence is in Ireland, whose regulator handles many cross-border privacy cases. The Garante rejected that argument because the ePrivacy rules at issue do not use that system.

Meta disagrees

Meta told Reuters that users must grant device permission before the feature can operate and can change that permission in their settings.

The social media company also called the fine, which amounts to less than 0.5% of global revenues, “disproportionate.” It will appeal, it told reporters.

The Garante attributed the amount of the fine to the high number of people affected (around 20 million Android users in Italy) along with the duration of the incident, which it referred to as a breach. It also called Meta out for its “poor level of cooperation.” Changes that the company made to its app were introduced late and only applied to users who update the app, it added.

Aside from the financial penalty, the regulator has ordered Meta to request consent separately for the camera roll suggestions feature. It must get that consent after explaining to users what it will use the data for and how to disable it. The company must turn it off by default even for those who previously gave the blanket permission, it said, and if it doesn’t comply by the 60-day deadline then it must not enable the feature for users who haven’t given consent.

The regulator is preparing for a potential follow-up. It has left the door open to address the possible use of content to train AI, which Meta has denied. The Garante also “reserves the right” to assess a new feature that allows the content of the camera roll to be processed in the cloud.

Meta announced an opt-in photo suggestions feature for the US and Canada in October 2025. It analyzes media to find memorable moments and suggests creative edits. Meta says suggestions remain private unless users choose to share them, and the feature can be turned off in Facebook’s camera roll settings.

What Facebook users can do

The Italian order does not automatically change permissions for users elsewhere, but you can review your own settings.

On Android, go to Settings > Apps > Facebook > Permissions > Photos and videos, then select Don’t allow to revoke gallery access. Depending on your Android version and the app, you may also have an option to allow access only to selected photos and videos. Menu names can vary by device.

While Italy’s decision didn’t target iPhone users, they can also review Facebook’s photo access under Settings > Privacy & Security > Photos.

Mobile protection, anywhere, anytime.

items.title: Holiday shopping in a world of fakes: How AI is changing the game
items.summary: It’s the most wonderful time of the year, especially for scammers. The holiday shopping season is packed with tempting one-day-only deals, gift guides, and retailers promising the perfect present at the perfect price. And wherever shoppers go, scammers aren’t far behind. Cybercriminals have always taken advantage of the holiday rush. Now AI makes it easier to create fake storefronts, products, reviews, and promotions that look and sound legitimate. For consumers, knowing what—and who—to trust is getting harder. Shoppers are worried. According to Malwarebytes research, 77% of consumers are concerned about being scammed by a retailer using a fake AI website, or using AI to misrepresent products or reviews. That concern is grounded in experience: More than one in four consumers (28%) have experienced an AI-related shopping scam in the past year Some were misled by AI-generated product photos or reviews. Others described ordering products that never arrived, sometimes from legitimate-looking websites that turned out to be fake. With the holiday shopping season upon us, we’re looking at how AI is changing the shopping experience, where consumers see risks and benefits, and how to shop more safely. When a great looking product isn’t what it seems Realistic product images, glowing reviews, and professional-looking websites can make unfamiliar retailers seem trustworthy. AI makes it easier to create all three in one polished package, which is convincing enough to deceive even careful shoppers. For some, these convincing fakes have made buying online feel unsettling. One survey respondent commented: “It seems as though when I’m shopping online, I notice the models are AI-generated or even the products themselves and that scares me. I can’t tell what’s real or not anymore. I don’t even know if what I’m looking to buy is real! I don’t know if what is being advertised is the actual product. AI is going too far.” Survey respondents shared real-life experiences that help explain those fears. One described receiving products that looked nothing like the photos: “I buy fewer items that I don’t already know from real life because I fell for manipulated images and the delivered items barely resembled the edited pictures in the shop!” This aligns with what we’re seeing too. As an example, earlier this year we found cat face flower seeds being sold online. But manipulated images don’t have to look this extreme, or this obvious. As AI improves, telling what’s genuine from what’s fake is getting much more difficult. Some of our survey respondents described seeing convincing fake storefronts that took their money without delivering anything: “It was a fake website promoting shoes. I bought them and it turned out to be an AI website. Now I’ll be more wary of these websites and what they look like.” These experiences are especially common among younger shoppers. 42% of Gen Z say they’ve experienced an AI-related shopping scam, compared with 30% of Millennials, 22% of Gen X, and just 9% of Boomers and older. The impact goes beyond lost money or a missing package. Respondents described feeling embarrassed, angry and unsettled by how convincing the deception was. For many, that experience left a lasting distrust of online retailers. How AI brings scams directly to shoppers Scammers don’t have to wait for shoppers to stumble across a fake website. With the help of AI, they can send convincing, personalized messages that appear to come from familiar brands, bringing scams directly to consumers. It’s no wonder that global mega-retailer Amazon is the most impersonated brand that we see in our threat intelligence data, followed by Walmart, Temu, Costco, and Steam. *Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026 Scammers are getting personal Nearly one in four consumers (24%) say they’ve received a scam message that felt highly personalised, sometimes including their name or other personal details. Among Gen Z, that figure rises to almost one in three (32%). We came across a scam that linked a person’s phone number and name with a fake Facebook Marketplace listing to act as a conversation lure and get them to respond. Answering a message is often the first step in what can become a very costly scam. Even when shoppers spot the warning signs, a personalised scam can leave them feeling uneasy. One respondent explained: “I received an email that was clearly directed to me personally, yet it seemed “off” which was an alarm for me. I investigated it before clicking on anything and knew then that it was a scam. It made me feel like nothing is safe out there anymore and you have to be hyper-alert at every moment when online.” Spotting scams among the shopping noise Delivery companies are an obvious choice for scammers to impersonate at this time of year. With more purchases being made, it can be hard to keep track of which retailer is using which delivery service, and on which date it will arrive. *Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026 Common delivery scam lures we’ve seen include: A delayed parcel notification, paired with a request to pay a small fee through a link A failed-delivery claim demanding address confirmation or rescheduling. Short deadlines or “final notice” language to create a sense of urgency. Lookalike delivery company domains and off-brand links. In this example, scammers use a fake missed delivery, the USPS brand, and a sense of urgency (48 hours) in order to get their target to click. The broader research shows just how challenging this environment has become: 85% agree that sophisticated scams can be hard to distinguish from the real thing 85% believe AI makes it easier for scammers and criminals to target people Even the most routine messages about purchases and deliveries warrant a closer look, and that’s one more thing for consumers to worry about during an already busy time of year. Where shoppers accept AI Despite their concerns, many consumers accept some uses of AI in retail. In the survey, 43% say it’s okay for businesses to use AI-generated websites to sell products, while 36% accept AI-generated salespeople. Including neutral responses, those figures rise to 72% and 64%, respectively. There’s also growing acceptance of AI on the retailer side. 43% say it’s okay for businesses to use AI-generated websites to sell products, while 36% are okay with AI-generated salespeople. Including those who feel neutral about these practices, the figures rise to 72% and 64%, respectively. That shows how willing consumers are to let AI into the shopping process, despite their concerns. That acceptance extends to product images: 60% say using AI to enhance them is no different from existing advertising practices. Product photos have long been staged, edited and polished to make merchandise look its best; AI can do the same. Shoppers’ responses show that concern about AI and acceptance of its use can coexist. In the holiday rush, distinguishing a useful shopping aid from a convincing deception can be difficult. Shoppers are taking precautions, but the burden is growing Some shoppers are responding in practical ways, starting with where they choose to buy: 36% have limited purchases from unfamiliar online retailers. 26% have limited purchases from social media accounts As one respondent explained: “I am more wary of purchasing something from an ad I see on social media. I tend to search for the item online myself and find a legit website to order from.” Others are checking information more carefully: One respondent described checking reviews on another website after watching a convincing product video on social media, only to uncover signs of a scam. Another now deliberately seeks out negative or neutral reviews and real customer photos. Others describe comparing information across multiple sources rather than taking any online content at face value. One respondent summed up the need for extra caution: “I tell my children not everything that glitters is gold. Always be careful and check everything yourself. With AI today you can make everything look beautiful but beautiful doesn’t mean true, correct or authentic. Fact checking is the order of the day.” Beyond checking information for themselves, consumers also value having another person to turn to when they need help. Nearly seven in ten (69%) say they’d spend extra time or pay more for human customer service, while 43% say they’ve tried to talk to a real person rather than an AI customer service system. AI may make shopping more convenient for some, but that doesn’t mean consumers want to rely on it for every interaction. How to spot AI-powered shopping scams this holiday season AI can make fake stores, product photos, and reviews look extremely convincing. Here are four ways to protect yourself: Slow down. Scammers use urgency to rush you. During the holidays, limited-time deals and delivery alerts can be especially persuasive. Don’t let a countdown or unexpected message stop you from checking first. Guard your information. Be wary of unexpected requests from sellers or delivery services for passwords, payment details, or other personal information. A message can use your name or mention a recent purchase and still be fake. You can check which data Verify the source. Check independent reviews and compare product photos and details across websites. Go to the retailer’s official site directly instead of following links in messages. Remember that logos, email addresses, and caller IDs can all be faked. Use anti-scam/scam detection tools. Malwarebytes offers free tools to help you spot and stop potential scams. If you’re worried about the legitimacy of a DM, text, email, link, or number, upload it to Scam Guard . We’ll give you a verdict on whether it’s safe, along with guidance on what to do next. You can also use Browser Guard as you shop to block scammy and fraudulent websites, and stop card skimmers in their tracks. About the research The research in this article is based on a March 2026 survey about AI, identity, and digital trust, conducted among 1,500 respondents in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. The research was prepared by an independent research consultant and distributed via Forsta. Something feel off? Check it before you click. items.summary_html:
It’s the most wonderful time of the year, especially for scammers. 

The holiday shopping season is packed with tempting one-day-only deals, gift guides, and retailers promising the perfect present at the perfect price. 

And wherever shoppers go, scammers aren’t far behind. 

Cybercriminals have always taken advantage of the holiday rush. Now AI makes it easier to create fake storefronts, products, reviews, and promotions that look and sound legitimate. For consumers, knowing what—and who—to trust is getting harder. 

Shoppers are worried. According to Malwarebytes research, 77% of consumers are concerned about being scammed by a retailer using a fake AI website, or using AI to misrepresent products or reviews.  

That concern is grounded in experience: More than one in four consumers (28%) have experienced an AI-related shopping scam in the past year Some were misled by AI-generated product photos or reviews. Others described ordering products that never arrived, sometimes from legitimate-looking websites that turned out to be fake. 

With the holiday shopping season upon us, we’re looking at how AI is changing the shopping experience, where consumers see risks and benefits, and how to shop more safely. 

When a great looking product isn’t what it seems 

Realistic product images, glowing reviews, and professional-looking websites can make unfamiliar retailers seem trustworthy. AI makes it easier to create all three in one polished package, which is convincing enough to deceive even careful shoppers. 

For some, these convincing fakes have made buying online feel unsettling. One survey respondent commented: 

“It seems as though when I’m shopping online, I notice the models are AI-generated or even the products themselves and that scares me. I can’t tell what’s real or not anymore. I don’t even know if what I’m looking to buy is real! I don’t know if what is being advertised is the actual product. AI is going too far.”   

Survey respondents shared real-life experiences that help explain those fears. One described receiving products that looked nothing like the photos: 

“I buy fewer items that I don’t already know from real life because I fell for manipulated images and the delivered items barely resembled the edited pictures in the shop!”  

This aligns with what we’re seeing too. As an example, earlier this year we found cat face flower seeds being sold online. 

But manipulated images don’t have to look this extreme, or this obvious. As AI improves, telling what’s genuine from what’s fake is getting much more difficult. 

Some of our survey respondents described seeing convincing fake storefronts that took their money without delivering anything: 

“It was a fake website promoting shoes. I bought them and it turned out to be an AI website. Now I’ll be more wary of these websites and what they look like.”

These experiences are especially common among younger shoppers. 42% of Gen Z say they’ve experienced an AI-related shopping scam, compared with 30% of Millennials, 22% of Gen X, and just 9% of Boomers and older. 

The impact goes beyond lost money or a missing package. Respondents described feeling embarrassed, angry and unsettled by how convincing the deception was. For many, that experience left a lasting distrust of online retailers. 

How AI brings scams directly to shoppers 

Scammers don’t have to wait for shoppers to stumble across a fake website. With the help of AI, they can send convincing, personalized messages that appear to come from familiar brands, bringing scams directly to consumers. 

It’s no wonder that global mega-retailer Amazon is the most impersonated brand that we see in our threat intelligence data, followed by Walmart, Temu, Costco, and Steam. 

*Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026  Scammers are getting personal 

Nearly one in four consumers (24%) say they’ve received a scam message that felt highly personalised, sometimes including their name or other personal details. Among Gen Z, that figure rises to almost one in three (32%). 

We came across a scam that linked a person’s phone number and name with a fake Facebook Marketplace listing to act as a conversation lure and get them to respond. Answering a message is often the first step in what can become a very costly scam. 

Even when shoppers spot the warning signs, a personalised scam can leave them feeling uneasy. One respondent explained: 

“I received an email that was clearly directed to me personally, yet it seemed “off” which was an alarm for me. I investigated it before clicking on anything and knew then that it was a scam. It made me feel like nothing is safe out there anymore and you have to be hyper-alert at every moment when online.” 

Spotting scams among the shopping noise 

Delivery companies are an obvious choice for scammers to impersonate at this time of year. With more purchases being made, it can be hard to keep track of which retailer is using which delivery service, and on which date it will arrive. 

*Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026 

Common delivery scam lures we’ve seen include: 

  • A delayed parcel notification, paired with a request to pay a small fee through a link
  • A failed-delivery claim demanding address confirmation or rescheduling.
  • Short deadlines or “final notice” language to create a sense of urgency.
  • Lookalike delivery company domains and off-brand links. 

In this example, scammers use a fake missed delivery, the USPS brand, and a sense of urgency (48 hours) in order to get their target to click.

The broader research shows just how challenging this environment has become: 

  • 85% agree that sophisticated scams can be hard to distinguish from the real thing 
  • 85% believe AI makes it easier for scammers and criminals to target people 

Even the most routine messages about purchases and deliveries warrant a closer look, and that’s one more thing for consumers to worry about during an already busy time of year. 

Where shoppers accept AI 

Despite their concerns, many consumers accept some uses of AI in retail. In the survey, 43% say it’s okay for businesses to use AI-generated websites to sell products, while 36% accept AI-generated salespeople. Including neutral responses, those figures rise to 72% and 64%, respectively. 

There’s also growing acceptance of AI on the retailer side. 43% say it’s okay for businesses to use AI-generated websites to sell products, while 36% are okay with AI-generated salespeople. Including those who feel neutral about these practices, the figures rise to 72% and 64%, respectively. That shows how willing consumers are to let AI into the shopping process, despite their concerns. 

That acceptance extends to product images: 60% say using AI to enhance them is no different from existing advertising practices. Product photos have long been staged, edited and polished to make merchandise look its best; AI can do the same. 

Shoppers’ responses show that concern about AI and acceptance of its use can coexist. In the holiday rush, distinguishing a useful shopping aid from a convincing deception can be difficult. 

Shoppers are taking precautions, but the burden is growing 

Some shoppers are responding in practical ways, starting with where they choose to buy: 

  • 36% have limited purchases from unfamiliar online retailers. 
  • 26% have limited purchases from social media accounts 

As one respondent explained: 

“I am more wary of purchasing something from an ad I see on social media. I tend to search for the item online myself and find a legit website to order from.”

Others are checking information more carefully: 

One respondent described checking reviews on another website after watching a convincing product video on social media, only to uncover signs of a scam. Another now deliberately seeks out negative or neutral reviews and real customer photos. Others describe comparing information across multiple sources rather than taking any online content at face value.  

One respondent summed up the need for extra caution: 

“I tell my children not everything that glitters is gold. Always be careful and check everything yourself. With AI today you can make everything look beautiful but beautiful doesn’t mean true, correct or authentic. Fact checking is the order of the day.”

Beyond checking information for themselves, consumers also value having another person to turn to when they need help. Nearly seven in ten (69%) say they’d spend extra time or pay more for human customer service, while 43% say they’ve tried to talk to a real person rather than an AI customer service system.

AI may make shopping more convenient for some, but that doesn’t mean consumers want to rely on it for every interaction.  

How to spot AI-powered shopping scams this holiday season 

AI can make fake stores, product photos, and reviews look extremely convincing. Here are four ways to protect yourself: 

  1. Slow down. Scammers use urgency to rush you. During the holidays, limited-time deals and delivery alerts can be especially persuasive. Don’t let a countdown or unexpected message stop you from checking first. 
  2. Guard your information. Be wary of unexpected requests from sellers or delivery services for passwords, payment details, or other personal information. A message can use your name or mention a recent purchase and still be fake. You can check which data
  3. Verify the source. Check independent reviews and compare product photos and details across websites. Go to the retailer’s official site directly instead of following links in messages. Remember that logos, email addresses, and caller IDs can all be faked. 
  4. Use anti-scam/scam detection tools. Malwarebytes offers free tools to help you spot and stop potential scams. If you’re worried about the legitimacy of a DM, text, email, link, or number, upload it to Scam Guard. We’ll give you a verdict on whether it’s safe, along with guidance on what to do next. About the research 

The research in this article is based on a March 2026 survey about AI, identity, and digital trust, conducted among 1,500 respondents in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. items.title: Chase Software Bug Disrupts Banking Services as Customers Report Outages at Major US Banks
items.summary: A software bug at JPMorgan Chase disrupted banking services on November 16, 2026, leaving thousands of customers reporting trouble with account access and payments. Complaints also appeared for Bank of America, Wells Fargo, U.S. Bank and Zelle, though reports did not establish separate outages at each bank. Chase linked the disruption to a temporary software issue in its “on-premise hardware systems,” meaning equipment within its own computing setup. The bank said there was no evidence of a cyberattack and described the problem as isolated rather than a failure across the wider banking system. Customers reported problems checking balances, viewing transactions and completing transfers. Some Chase users also faced trouble withdrawing money, while delays affected both online services and branch transactions. Chase said customers retained access to their accounts and funds, although some requests were taking longer than usual to complete. Chase Outage Affected Other Banks The wider impact came from transactions involving Chase, not confirmed failures inside every bank named in customer complaints. Chase said other institutions could experience slower processing when it was involved in a payment. Bank of America and Citigroup were not experiencing failures in their own banking services. U.S. Bank made a similar distinction, saying its systems were not directly affected. Customers sending or receiving Zelle payments involving another financial institution could still face delays. This explains why reports across several banking brands did not mean every institution had suffered its own technical failure. Zelle said its network was “operating as it should.” Its operator, Early Warning Services, linked delayed payments to problems at financial institutions. As the Associated Press explained , customers using other banks could encounter delays when sending money to, or receiving money from, a Chase customer. The available evidence points to a service availability problem, not a confirmed data breach. CNN reported that an update to Chase’s physical computer systems caused the issue, citing a person familiar with the matter. Chase’s public explanation identified a software bug without naming the affected component or releasing a detailed technical report. That distinction matters when assessing banking disruptions. Cyber Security News previously covered DDoS attacks causing financial-sector outages , but Chase reported no evidence of such activity here. The incident also followed the separate Microsoft 365 service outage , with no established connection between the two events. Chase Reports Recovery By Monday evening, Chase said transactions were posting normally, according to NBC News . The recovery update marked an improvement after hours of customer complaints. It did not provide a full breakdown of the software fault, leaving the exact failure mechanism and steps to prevent a repeat unclear. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Hackers Infect 178 Major Websites via Optimizely to Steal Credit Cards and Target iPhones
items.summary: On 16 November 2026, attackers planted malicious JavaScript inside the Optimizely Web experimentation platform. The code reached visitors of 178 organizations. The list includes some of the busiest sites on the internet, such as Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock. Researcher Scott Helme of Report URI found the campaign. He confirmed that crypto has already been stolen and traced the transactions to wallets controlled by the attackers. This was not a simple skimmer. The malware worked as a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses, stole payment card details, grabbed cookies and screenshots, and pushed the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits to iPhone and iPad users. What makes the case worrying is that none of the affected websites had to be hacked directly. The bad code came through a trusted third-party script that each site loaded on every page. Optimizely Snippet Was Abused Optimizely Web works by having each customer load a JavaScript “snippet” from cdn.optimizely.com. The file holds Optimizely’s code, the customer’s experiments, and an optional field called Project JavaScript. Optimizely’s documentation says Project JavaScript is the first code to run in the snippet and can affect every experiment in a project. The attacker wrote a small loader into this field and left the rest of the snippet untouched. The file was still served from Optimizely’s domain with Optimizely’s certificate, so browsers and security tools treated it as normal. In Zoom’s snippet, the added code quietly created a new script tag that pulled a file called track.js from the domain 1688360.cc. Report URI found three versions of the loader. Most snippets used a plain script tag. Others hid the same URL in base64 with atob(), so a simple search for “1688360.cc” would miss it. A third version carried a full inline copy of the payload and ran it through eval if the attacker’s domain was blocked. Smartsheet cleaned the snippet at one point, then re-infected it with the base64 version, showing the attacker still had access. Sites that serve the snippet from their own domain, such as Scheels and Vodafone Australia, were also affected because the content came from the same Optimizely project. What the Malware Stole The crypto clipper scanned each page for wallet addresses on Bitcoin, Ethereum, TRON, Solana, TON, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash and Dogecoin. It swapped them for attacker addresses in page text, in the clipboard, and in outgoing web requests. By 19:25 UTC, the attacker’s wallets had received about $7,040. Stolen funds were moved to exchanges at around 13:03 UTC. The attacker added a card skimmer at 13:43 UTC. It watched form submissions for a card number, expiry date and CVV, then sent the details to 1688360.cc/card.php. Cards typed into hosted payment frames such as Stripe or Adyen were out of its reach. Cards entered into a site’s own form fields were not. The script also sent page URLs, readable cookies and html2canvas screenshots to 1688360.cc/hit.php. iPhones Targeted With Coruna and DarkSword On Apple mobile devices, the script loaded a router file from .icu domains and chose an exploit chain based on the iOS version. Devices on iOS 13 to 17 received Coruna. Devices on iOS 18 received DarkSword. A separate chain for iOS 26 only fingerprinted the device. Google’s Threat Intelligence Group says Coruna contains 23 exploits across five full chains. DarkSword links six vulnerabilities against iOS 18.4 to 18.7 . Readers can find more background in our earlier reports on the Coruna exploit kit and the DarkSword iOS exploit chain . Indicators of Compromise Indicator Role 1688360.cc (136.113.106.136) C2 hosting track.js, card.php, hit.php 5vobauua3ojpklx.icu (34.96.213.201) iOS router boot.js eil786npto9u5bq.icu (34.87.36.58) iOS router and Coruna pages l7bcsnwc7nzr3uo.icu Coruna telemetry webshell.lol Injector from an earlier wave f7b84b9a94f749f8ced3f0112d0a66894e8bbc3b4aa5592021d1b8976a9bad40 SHA-256 of the latest track.js build Report URI says it does not know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects. The researchers ruled out CDN cache poisoning. The snippets for Optimizely’s own sites, including login.optimizely.com, also carried the malicious code. Report URI said it had not heard back from Optimizely when it published its findings. Most of the code was gone by 21:52 UTC, when only TalkTalk’s snippet was still infected, down from 169 at 20:56 UTC. Optimizely Web customers should open every Project JavaScript field and every experiment’s custom code. They should look for 1688360.cc, atob( and any script they did not write. Optimizely’s change history logs all Project JavaScript changes. It also shows whether each change came through the REST API or the web interface. Teams should review users, API tokens and integrations, then rotate their credentials. Cards entered on 16 November, and any secrets stored in non-HttpOnly cookies, should be treated as exposed. Content Security Policy made a clear difference. Of the affected organizations whose own websites Report URI checked, 68 had no CSP at all, and only 24 blocked the payload completely. Allowing ‘unsafe-eval’ or ‘strict-dynamic’ let the code through. Users should update to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later. They should also double-check any crypto transfers and card statements from that day. Update: Optimizely said it contained the Web Experimentation incident, blocked the vulnerable path, removed injected code, and contacted affected customers directly. Further updates are available on its status page . Earlier today, Optimizely identified and contained a security incident affecting some Optimizely Web Experimentation customers. The vulnerable path is blocked, the injected code was removed, and customers have been contacted directly. Updates: https://t.co/ptZHZviIeC — Optimizely (@Optimizely) November 17, 2026 Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: CVE-2026-104692 / CVE-2026-104007 - LibreOffice RCE via ODF Form Datasource JDBC Code Execution
items.summary: Introduction This blog post describes how to exploit a remote code execution vulnerability in LibreOffice by combining two security vulnerabilities with several ODF document features to build a complete exploit chain. The exploit achieves arbitrary command execution on macOS, Windows, and Linux when a victim simply opens a crafted spreadsheet file, with no user interaction, no macro warning, and no security prompt. The vulnerabilities are tracked as CVE-2026-104692 and CVE-2026-104007. Affected Versions Affected Fixed Prerequisite ≤ 26.2.6.x 26.2.7 Java runtime installed and enabled in LibreOffice ≤ 26.8.1 26.8.2 Java runtime installed and enabled in LibreOffice Vulnerability Two independent vulnerabilities make this exploit possible. CVE-2026-104007 alone is sufficient for RCE via the Driver.connect() path, which bypasses the HSQLDB method whitelist entirely. The exploit demonstrates this on Linux, while on macOS and Windows it chains both CVEs through the HSQLDB CALL path. CVE-2026-104692: HSQLDB Method Whitelist Not Enforced The HSQLDB bundled with LibreOffice has a method whitelist mechanism in HsqlDatabaseProperties.supportsJavaMethod() that controls which Java methods can be invoked through SQL CALL statements. At [A], the whitelist field accessibleJavaMethodNames is initialized to null instead of an empty set. At [B], since the field is null , supportsJavaMethod() unconditionally returns true for any method name — effectively disabling the entire whitelist and allowing arbitrary Java method execution through HSQLDB. The static initializer at [C] reads System.getProperty("hsqldb.method_class_names") and parses semicolon-separated method names to populate the whitelist. But since the field starts as null (not an empty set), supportsJavaMethod() already returns true regardless of whether this code runs. // org/hsqldb/persist/HsqlDatabaseProperties.java public class HsqlDatabaseProperties extends HsqlProperties { private static HashSet accessibleJavaMethodNames = null ; // [A] null = allow all // ... public static boolean supportsJavaMethod ( String string ) { if ( accessibleJavaMethodNames == null ) { // [B] always true when null return true ; // ALL methods allowed } if ( string . startsWith ( "org.hsqldb.Library." )) return true ; if ( string . startsWith ( "java.lang.Math." )) return true ; if ( accessibleJavaMethodNames . contains ( string )) return true ; Iterator iterator = accessibleJavaMethodNames . iterator (); while ( iterator . hasNext ()) { String string2 = ( String ) iterator . next (); int n = string2 . lastIndexOf ( ".*" ); if ( n < 1 || ! string . startsWith ( string2 . substring ( 0 , n + 1 ))) continue ; return true ; } return false ; } // ... static { try { String string = System . getProperty ( "hsqldb.method_class_names" ); // [C] if ( string != null ) { String [] stringArray = StringUtil . split ( string , ";" ); for ( int i = 0 ; i < stringArray . length ; ++ i ) { accessibleJavaMethodNames . add ( stringArray [ i ]); } } } catch ( Exception exception ) {} // ... meta initialization } } When HSQLDB processes a CALL statement, Database.getJavaName() resolves the method name. At [D], it calls supportsJavaMethod() to check whether the method is allowed. Because the whitelist is null , this check always passes, and any Java method — including the attacker’s evil.Driver.pwn() — is invoked without restriction. // org/hsqldb/Database.java class Database { // ... private HHashMap hAlias ; String getJavaName ( String string ) throws HsqlException { String string2 = ( String ) this . hAlias . get ( string ); if ( string2 == null ) { string2 = string ; } if ( HsqlDatabaseProperties . supportsJavaMethod ( string2 )) { // [D] always passes return string2 ; } throw Trace . error ( 33 , string2 ); } // ... } CVE-2026-104007: setPropertyInfo Bypass for External ODB References dbaxml::ODBFilter::setPropertyInfo() is a security function that strips the JavaDriverClassPath property from ODB files during XML import to prevent attacker-controlled classpath injection. At [E], when an ODB is opened directly, setPropertyInfo() removes the dangerous property after XML parsing but before properties are applied to the datasource. // dbaccess/source/filter/xml/xmlfilter.cxx void ODBFilter :: setPropertyInfo () { // ... :: comphelper :: NamedValueCollection aDocumentSettings ( aInfo ); aDocumentSettings . remove ( u"JavaDriverClassPath" _ustr ); // [E] strips classpath aDataSourceSettings . merge ( aDocumentSettings , true ); // ... } However, setPropertyInfo() is called only when directly opening an ODB file . When an ODB is referenced as an external datasource via form:datasource , this filter is not invoked. At [F], the ODB’s db:java-classpath is passed directly to JConnection::construct() and loaded into the URLClassLoader with the attacker’s classpath intact. This bypass is critical because it allows the attacker to control which classes URLClassLoader loads — without a classpath, even if CVE-2026-104692 allows calling arbitrary methods, there are no attacker-controlled classes to call. // connectivity/source/drivers/jdbc/JConnection.cxx — construct() sDriverClassPath = aSettings . getOrDefault ( u"JavaDriverClassPath" _ustr , sDriverClassPath ); // [F] classpath NOT stripped if ( sDriverClassPath . isEmpty () ) sDriverClassPath = impl_getJavaDriverClassPath_nothrow ( sDriverClass ); // ... loadDriverFromProperties ( sDriverClass , sDriverClassPath , aSystemProperties ); ODB Import Pipeline: Direct ODB open: ODBFilter::filter() → ODBFilter::implImport() → ReadThroughComponent() ← XML parsed, classpath loaded → setPropertyInfo() ← [E] strips JavaDriverClassPath → properties applied to datasource External ODB via form:datasource: form auto-load triggered → HTTP GET payload.odb → ODB loaded into datasource → setPropertyInfo() NOT called ← [F] classpath preserved! → properties applied with attacker's classpath intact Patch The 26.8.2.2 pre-release patches both vulnerabilities with defense-in-depth. CVE-2026-104692 : accessibleJavaMethodNames is initialized to an empty HashSet instead of null , so supportsJavaMethod() falls through to the whitelist check and blocks all methods not in org.hsqldb.Library.* or java.lang.Math.* . The static initializer still reads System.getProperty("hsqldb.method_class_names") after creating the empty set, but since LibreOffice does not set this property, the set remains empty. --- a/hsqldb/src/org/hsqldb/persist/HsqlDatabaseProperties.java +++ b/hsqldb/src/org/hsqldb/persist/HsqlDatabaseProperties.java @@ -57,15 +57,13 @@ private static String hsqldb_method_class_names = "hsqldb.method_class_names"; - private static HashSet accessibleJavaMethodNames; + private static HashSet accessibleJavaMethodNames = new HashSet(); static { try { String prop = System.getProperty(hsqldb_method_class_names); if (prop != null) { - accessibleJavaMethodNames = new HashSet(); - String[] names = StringUtil.split(prop, ";"); for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) { @@ -76,11 +74,9 @@ } /** - * If the system property "hsqldb.method_class_names" is not set, then - * static methods of all available Java classes can be accessed as functions - * in HSQLDB. If the property is set, then only the list of semicolon - * seperated method names becomes accessible. An empty property value means - * no class is accessible. + * Only the semicolon seperated method names in the system property + * "hsqldb.method_class_names" are accessible. An empty or unset property + * means no class is accessible. * * A property value that ends with .* is treated as a wild card and allows * access to all classe or method names formed by substitution of the CVE-2026-104007 : Two defense-in-depth changes were added. First, setPropertyInfo() now also strips SystemProperties from ODB files during XML import, closing a system property injection vector where an attacker could set hsqldb.method_class_names via the ODB’s db:data-source-settings to re-populate the whitelist bypassed by CVE-2026-104692. --- a/dbaccess/source/filter/xml/xmlfilter.cxx +++ b/dbaccess/source/filter/xml/xmlfilter.cxx void ODBFilter::setPropertyInfo() { // ... ::comphelper::NamedValueCollection aDocumentSettings( aInfo ); - // The Java class path of a driver comes from the driver configuration, not the document. + // The Java class path of a driver and the Java system properties come from the driver + // configuration, not the document. aDocumentSettings.remove( u"JavaDriverClassPath"_ustr ); + aDocumentSettings.remove( u"SystemProperties"_ustr ); // CreateDatabase asks the driver for a new database, which only the user does from the UI. aDocumentSettings.remove( u"CreateDatabase"_ustr ); aDataSourceSettings.merge( aDocumentSettings, true ); // ... } Second, the datasource connection path now checks whether the document is in a trusted location. Untrusted documents have their additional driver options ( INFO_ADDITIONALOPTIONS ) filtered out during connection setup, and ADO connections from untrusted locations are blocked entirely. --- a/dbaccess/source/core/dataaccess/datasource.cxx +++ b/dbaccess/source/core/dataaccess/datasource.cxx Sequence< PropertyValue > lcl_filterDriverProperties( const Reference< XDriver >& _xDriver, const OUString& _sUrl, - const Sequence< PropertyValue >& _rDataSourceSettings ) + const Sequence< PropertyValue >& _rDataSourceSettings, bool bTrustedLocation ) { // ... for (auto& dataSourceSetting : _rDataSourceSettings) { + // Additional driver options follow the same rule as updating links. + if (!bTrustedLocation && dataSourceSetting.Name == INFO_ADDITIONALOPTIONS) + continue; // ... } } Defense-in-Depth The patches create overlapping defense layers. Even if one layer is bypassed, the others independently block the attack. Layer 1: setPropertyInfo() — strips from ODB XML ├── JavaDriverClassPath → removed (no class loading) ├── SystemProperties → removed (no property injection) └── CreateDatabase → removed (no DB at arbitrary path) Layer 2: Trusted Location Check — datasource.cxx ├── Untrusted documents have additional driver options filtered └── ADO connections blocked from untrusted locations Layer 3: HSQLDB Method Whitelist ├── accessibleJavaMethodNames = new HashSet() (empty, not null) ├── Only org.hsqldb.Library.* and java.lang.Math.* allowed └── System.getProperty("hsqldb.method_class_names") checked at class load Even if classpath survives → whitelist blocks CALL → no method execution Even if whitelist bypassed → trusted location check limits driver options Even if SystemProperties injected → stripping prevents whitelist repopulation Exploitation The exploit reaches the two vulnerabilities above through a chain of ODF document features that, while not vulnerabilities themselves, enable the attack to trigger automatically. Opening the document is enough — no macros, no prompts, no additional interaction required. Exploit Chain The exploit leverages five ODF/LibreOffice features to deliver the payload and trigger the two vulnerabilities without user interaction: 1. HTTP ODB Auto-Download — ODF documents can reference an external database file (ODB) through form:datasource . When this attribute contains an HTTP URL, LibreOffice downloads the ODB file from the remote server without user confirmation. This delivers the attacker’s ODB payload containing the malicious classpath configuration (CVE-2026-104007). 2. Form Auto-Load — The form:apply-design-mode="false" attribute causes LibreOffice to automatically connect to the datasource and execute the form’s SQL command upon document open. LibreOffice classifies database access as a non-macro operation, so no macro security dialog is triggered. 3. SQL Composer Bypass — The form:escape-processing="false" attribute disables SingleSelectQueryComposer validation, allowing CALL statements to reach HSQLDB unmodified. Without this, the SQL composer would reject the CALL syntax as it only handles SELECT statements. 4. ODS-as-Class-Container — Since ODS files are ZIP archives, the attacker embeds the malicious evil/Driver.class directly inside the ODS file itself. Java’s URLClassLoader treats ZIP/JAR files as class containers and loads .class files from them. The ODB payload sets the classpath to point back to this file on disk. 5. Bootstrap Variable Path Prediction — LibreOffice supports bootstrap variables ( $SYSUSERHOME , ${.envvar:HOME} ) in classpath strings that resolve to platform-specific user directories at runtime. The attacker lists multiple common download locations (Downloads, Desktop, Documents) — URLClassLoader silently ignores paths that don’t exist, so one will match regardless of where the victim saved the file. The crafted ODS file combines all five features. At [A], it references the attacker’s HTTP server. At [B], it enables form auto-load. items.summary_html:
Introduction

This blog post describes how to exploit a remote code execution vulnerability in LibreOffice by combining two security vulnerabilities with several ODF document features to build a complete exploit chain. The exploit achieves arbitrary command execution on macOS, Windows, and Linux when a victim simply opens a crafted spreadsheet file, with no user interaction, no macro warning, and no security prompt.
The vulnerabilities are tracked as CVE-2026-104692 and CVE-2026-104007.


Affected Versions Affected Fixed Prerequisite ≤ 26.2.6.x 26.2.7 Java runtime installed and enabled in LibreOffice ≤ 26.8.1 26.8.2 Java runtime installed and enabled in LibreOffice


Vulnerability

Two independent vulnerabilities make this exploit possible. CVE-2026-104007 alone is sufficient for RCE via the Driver.connect() path, which bypasses the HSQLDB method whitelist entirely. The exploit demonstrates this on Linux, while on macOS and Windows it chains both CVEs through the HSQLDB CALL path.


CVE-2026-104692: HSQLDB Method Whitelist Not Enforced

The HSQLDB bundled with LibreOffice has a method whitelist mechanism in HsqlDatabaseProperties.supportsJavaMethod() that controls which Java methods can be invoked through SQL CALL statements. At [A], the whitelist field accessibleJavaMethodNames is initialized to null instead of an empty set. At [B], since the field is null, supportsJavaMethod() unconditionally returns true for any method name — effectively disabling the entire whitelist and allowing arbitrary Java method execution through HSQLDB.

The static initializer at [C] reads System.getProperty("hsqldb.method_class_names") and parses semicolon-separated method names to populate the whitelist. But since the field starts as null (not an empty set), supportsJavaMethod() already returns true regardless of whether this code runs.

// org/hsqldb/persist/HsqlDatabaseProperties.java

public class HsqlDatabaseProperties extends HsqlProperties {

    private static HashSet accessibleJavaMethodNames = null;  // [A] null = allow all

    // ...

    public static boolean supportsJavaMethod(String string) {
        if (accessibleJavaMethodNames == null) {  // [B] always true when null
            return true;                          // ALL methods allowed
        }
        if (string.startsWith("org.hsqldb.Library.")) return true;
        if (string.startsWith("java.lang.Math.")) return true;
        if (accessibleJavaMethodNames.contains(string)) return true;
        Iterator iterator = accessibleJavaMethodNames.iterator();
        while (iterator.hasNext()) {
            String string2 = (String)iterator.next();
            int n = string2.lastIndexOf(".*");
            if (n < 1 || !string.startsWith(string2.substring(0, n + 1))) continue;
            return true;
        }
        return false;
    }

    // ...

    static {
        try {
            String string = System.getProperty("hsqldb.method_class_names");  // [C]
            if (string != null) {
                String[] stringArray = StringUtil.split(string, ";");
                for (int i = 0; i < stringArray.length; ++i) {
                    accessibleJavaMethodNames.add(stringArray[i]);
                }
            }
        } catch (Exception exception) {}
        // ... meta initialization
    }
}


When HSQLDB processes a CALL statement, Database.getJavaName() resolves the method name. At [D], it calls supportsJavaMethod() to check whether the method is allowed. Because the whitelist is null, this check always passes, and any Java method — including the attacker’s evil.Driver.pwn() — is invoked without restriction.

// org/hsqldb/Database.java

class Database {

    // ...

    private HHashMap hAlias;

    String getJavaName(String string) throws HsqlException {
        String string2 = (String)this.hAlias.get(string);
        if (string2 == null) {
            string2 = string;
        }
        if (HsqlDatabaseProperties.supportsJavaMethod(string2)) {  // [D] always passes
            return string2;
        }
        throw Trace.error(33, string2);
    }

    // ...
}


CVE-2026-104007: setPropertyInfo Bypass for External ODB References

dbaxml::ODBFilter::setPropertyInfo() is a security function that strips the JavaDriverClassPath property from ODB files during XML import to prevent attacker-controlled classpath injection. At [E], when an ODB is opened directly, setPropertyInfo() removes the dangerous property after XML parsing but before properties are applied to the datasource.

// dbaccess/source/filter/xml/xmlfilter.cxx

void ODBFilter::setPropertyInfo()
{
    // ...
    ::comphelper::NamedValueCollection aDocumentSettings( aInfo );
    aDocumentSettings.remove( u"JavaDriverClassPath"_ustr );     // [E] strips classpath
    aDataSourceSettings.merge( aDocumentSettings, true );
    // ...
}


However, setPropertyInfo() is called only when directly opening an ODB file. When an ODB is referenced as an external datasource via form:datasource, this filter is not invoked. At [F], the ODB’s db:java-classpath is passed directly to JConnection::construct() and loaded into the URLClassLoader with the attacker’s classpath intact. This bypass is critical because it allows the attacker to control which classes URLClassLoader loads — without a classpath, even if CVE-2026-104692 allows calling arbitrary methods, there are no attacker-controlled classes to call.

// connectivity/source/drivers/jdbc/JConnection.cxx — construct()

sDriverClassPath = aSettings.getOrDefault(
    u"JavaDriverClassPath"_ustr, sDriverClassPath);  // [F] classpath NOT stripped
if ( sDriverClassPath.isEmpty() )
    sDriverClassPath = impl_getJavaDriverClassPath_nothrow(sDriverClass);
// ...
loadDriverFromProperties( sDriverClass, sDriverClassPath, aSystemProperties );

ODB Import Pipeline:

Direct ODB open:
  ODBFilter::filter()
    → ODBFilter::implImport()
      → ReadThroughComponent()          ← XML parsed, classpath loaded
      → setPropertyInfo()               ← [E] strips JavaDriverClassPath
      → properties applied to datasource

External ODB via form:datasource:
  form auto-load triggered
    → HTTP GET payload.odb
    → ODB loaded into datasource
    → setPropertyInfo() NOT called      ← [F] classpath preserved!
    → properties applied with attacker's classpath intact


Patch

The 26.8.2.2 pre-release patches both vulnerabilities with defense-in-depth.


CVE-2026-104692: accessibleJavaMethodNames is initialized to an empty HashSet instead of null, so supportsJavaMethod() falls through to the whitelist check and blocks all methods not in org.hsqldb.Library.* or java.lang.Math.*. The static initializer still reads System.getProperty("hsqldb.method_class_names") after creating the empty set, but since LibreOffice does not set this property, the set remains empty.

CVE-2026-104007: Two defense-in-depth changes were added. First, setPropertyInfo() now also strips SystemProperties from ODB files during XML import, closing a system property injection vector where an attacker could set hsqldb.method_class_names via the ODB’s db:data-source-settings to re-populate the whitelist bypassed by CVE-2026-104692.

--- a/dbaccess/source/filter/xml/xmlfilter.cxx
+++ b/dbaccess/source/filter/xml/xmlfilter.cxx
 void ODBFilter::setPropertyInfo()
 {
     // ...
     ::comphelper::NamedValueCollection aDocumentSettings( aInfo );
-    // The Java class path of a driver comes from the driver configuration, not the document.
+    // The Java class path of a driver and the Java system properties come from the driver
+    // configuration, not the document.
     aDocumentSettings.remove( u"JavaDriverClassPath"_ustr );
+    aDocumentSettings.remove( u"SystemProperties"_ustr );
     // CreateDatabase asks the driver for a new database, which only the user does from the UI.
     aDocumentSettings.remove( u"CreateDatabase"_ustr );
     aDataSourceSettings.merge( aDocumentSettings, true );
     // ...
 }


Second, the datasource connection path now checks whether the document is in a trusted location. Untrusted documents have their additional driver options (INFO_ADDITIONALOPTIONS) filtered out during connection setup, and ADO connections from untrusted locations are blocked entirely.

--- a/dbaccess/source/core/dataaccess/datasource.cxx
+++ b/dbaccess/source/core/dataaccess/datasource.cxx

     const OUString& _sUrl,
-    const Sequence< PropertyValue >& _rDataSourceSettings )
+    const Sequence< PropertyValue >& _rDataSourceSettings, bool bTrustedLocation )
 {
     // ...
     for (auto& dataSourceSetting : _rDataSourceSettings)
     {
+        // Additional driver options follow the same rule as updating links.
+        if (!bTrustedLocation && dataSourceSetting.Name == INFO_ADDITIONALOPTIONS)
+            continue;
         // ...
     }
 }


Defense-in-Depth

The patches create overlapping defense layers. Even if one layer is bypassed, the others independently block the attack.

Layer 1: setPropertyInfo() — strips from ODB XML
  ├── JavaDriverClassPath → removed (no class loading)
  ├── SystemProperties    → removed (no property injection)
  └── CreateDatabase      → removed (no DB at arbitrary path)

Layer 2: Trusted Location Check — datasource.cxx
  ├── Untrusted documents have additional driver options filtered
  └── ADO connections blocked from untrusted locations

Layer 3: HSQLDB Method Whitelist
  ├── accessibleJavaMethodNames = new HashSet() (empty, not null)
  ├── Only org.hsqldb.Library.* and java.lang.Math.* allowed
  └── System.getProperty("hsqldb.method_class_names") checked at class load

Even if classpath survives → whitelist blocks CALL → no method execution
Even if whitelist bypassed → trusted location check limits driver options
Even if SystemProperties injected → stripping prevents whitelist repopulation


Exploitation

The exploit reaches the two vulnerabilities above through a chain of ODF document features that, while not vulnerabilities themselves, enable the attack to trigger automatically. Opening the document is enough — no macros, no prompts, no additional interaction required.


Exploit Chain

The exploit leverages five ODF/LibreOffice features to deliver the payload and trigger the two vulnerabilities without user interaction:

1. HTTP ODB Auto-Download — ODF documents can reference an external database file (ODB) through form:datasource. When this attribute contains an HTTP URL, LibreOffice downloads the ODB file from the remote server without user confirmation. This delivers the attacker’s ODB payload containing the malicious classpath configuration (CVE-2026-104007).

2. Form Auto-Load — The form:apply-design-mode="false" attribute causes LibreOffice to automatically connect to the datasource and execute the form’s SQL command upon document open. LibreOffice classifies database access as a non-macro operation, so no macro security dialog is triggered.

3. SQL Composer Bypass — The form:escape-processing="false" attribute disables SingleSelectQueryComposer validation, allowing CALL statements to reach HSQLDB unmodified. Without this, the SQL composer would reject the CALL syntax as it only handles SELECT statements.

4. ODS-as-Class-Container — Since ODS files are ZIP archives, the attacker embeds the malicious evil/Driver.class directly inside the ODS file itself. Java’s URLClassLoader treats ZIP/JAR files as class containers and loads .class files from them. The ODB payload sets the classpath to point back to this file on disk.

5. Bootstrap Variable Path Prediction — LibreOffice supports bootstrap variables ($SYSUSERHOME, ${.envvar:HOME}) in classpath strings that resolve to platform-specific user directories at runtime. The attacker lists multiple common download locations (Downloads, Desktop, Documents) — URLClassLoader silently ignores paths that don’t exist, so one will match regardless of where the victim saved the file.


The crafted ODS file combines all five features. At [A], it references the attacker’s HTTP server. At [B], it enables form auto-load. At [C], it disables SQL composer validation.
